title: The Energy Transition Has a Speed Advantage That Cost Models Miss | OilPrice.com
description:
Electricity demand is accelerating, driven by data centers, electrification, new factories and cooling.
A power plant that is cheap in 2035 cannot supply a data center that wants to connect in 2028.
The equivalent assumptions are approximately two years for a new combined-cycle gas plant, five to five-and-a-half years for coal and seven years for nuclear.
But the idea that planners can simply order a large gas plant whenever demand appears is outdated.
A gas or nuclear plant can generate through the night and during windless weather.
text:
Power technologies are usually compared by asking how much their electricity costs. That is no longer enough.

Electricity demand is accelerating, driven by data centers, electrification, new factories and cooling. The International Energy Agency expects global data-center consumption alone to more than double to around 945 TWh by 2030—slightly more than Japan consumes today.

A power plant that is cheap in 2035 cannot supply a data center that wants to connect in 2028. As demand begins arriving faster than conventional generating capacity, time-to-power is becoming almost as important as levelized cost.

This creates an advantage for renewables that conventional comparisons routinely miss.

Solar and wind are not only increasingly cheap. They are modular, repeatable and unusually fast to build. In an electricity system suddenly short of both power and time, that may matter more than any cost forecast.

Solar Can Arrive Before the Forecast Changes Again

Lazard’s 2025 cost assumptions put the construction period for utility-scale solar at around 15 months, onshore wind at 18 months and offshore wind at 24 months. Distributed rooftop solar can be installed in days once approvals and equipment are available.

The equivalent assumptions are approximately two years for a new combined-cycle gas plant, five to five-and-a-half years for coal and seven years for nuclear. Full project development, including planning and permitting, can be much longer for every technology.

These are not hard limits. A badly permitted solar farm can spend years in development, while standardized gas plants can sometimes move faster. China has also built coal and nuclear plants faster than Western economies generally manage. Related: Hormuz Blockage Puts Qatar's $83 Billion LNG Bet at Risk

But renewables have a structural advantage: they consist of thousands of manufactured units that can be installed in parallel. A solar farm does not require one enormous reactor pressure vessel, boiler or turbine around which the entire project schedule revolves. Capacity can be added in phases, and the first part can begin generating before the whole development is complete.

That changes investment risk as well as construction speed.

A project that starts producing after 18 months generates revenue while a slower alternative is still consuming capital. Shorter construction reduces exposure to interest rates, inflation, regulatory changes and cost overruns. If demand forecasts change, a modular project can be resized or stopped between phases. A half-built nuclear or coal plant offers no comparable flexibility. Speed is therefore not merely an engineering characteristic. It is a financial advantage.

Gas Turbines Are Joining the Queue

Gas has traditionally been the obvious answer when a power system needed firm capacity quickly. Combined-cycle plants were relatively standardized, smaller and faster to build than coal or nuclear, while simple-cycle turbines could be deployed even faster. The data-center boom is now squeezing that advantage.

Siemens Energy shipped 6 GW of turbines during its fiscal third quarter of 2026, yet finished the period with a 69-GW gas-turbine backlog. Company executives said lead times were running at three years or more.

GE Vernova’s position is even more striking. Its gas-power equipment backlog and slot reservations reached 116 GW in the second quarter of 2026, up from 100 GW only three months earlier. The company is already taking reservations for delivery in 2031.

The bottleneck is not just construction. A developer must obtain a scarce turbine, then secure engineering capacity, financing, permits, a gas connection and grid access. Reuters reported in March that combined-cycle costs had more than doubled to above $2,400 per kilowatt, while turbine lead times exceeded five years in parts of the market.

Gas will remain essential in many systems because it can produce when wind and solar cannot. Existing gas plants may also be uprated or used more intensively much faster than new capacity can be built.

But the idea that planners can simply order a large gas plant whenever demand appears is outdated. The turbine slot may arrive after the customer it was intended to serve.

Capacity Is Not the Same as Dependable Power

The strongest objection is obvious. One gigawatt of solar is not equivalent to one gigawatt of nuclear or gas.

A gas or nuclear plant can generate through the night and during windless weather. Solar output depends on daylight, while wind output depends on weather. Comparing nameplate capacity without accounting for generation, timing and reliability exaggerates what renewables can deliver. That criticism is correct.

Rapid renewable construction does not eliminate the need for firm capacity, storage, transmission and flexible demand. Nor does a completed solar farm help if it waits five years for a grid connection. The IEA estimates that more than 2,500 GW of renewable, storage and large-load projects are stalled in queues worldwide. New transmission can take five to 15 years.

But this does not erase the speed advantage. It defines how to use it. Solar and wind can provide the bulk energy quickly. Batteries can shift several hours of production into evening peaks and provide grid services. Existing hydro, nuclear and gas fleets can supply firm capacity while demand response reduces the size of the peak. New firm low-carbon technologies can then be developed for the longer term without pretending they will solve a shortage arriving this decade.

The relevant comparison is not solar alone versus a combined-cycle gas plant. It is the fastest buildable portfolio versus waiting for one supposedly perfect asset.

The Market Is Already Choosing What Can Be Delivered

Deployment is increasingly reflecting this reality. The IEA expects renewables to supply nearly half of the additional electricity consumed by data centers through 2035, explicitly citing their short lead times, competitiveness and compatibility with corporate power-purchase agreements.

US developers are also turning to solar-plus-storage because gas turbines are difficult to obtain. Hybrid projects can now be completed in roughly 18 to 20 months in favorable markets. They do not provide unlimited backup, but they can deliver substantial volumes of electricity before a new turbine leaves the factory.

This is why the response to accelerating demand cannot consist only of announcing more power plants. Governments and grid operators must prioritize projects capable of reaching operation, not merely projects that look attractive in capacity plans.

That means reforming grid queues so mature projects replace speculative reservations, pre-permitting suitable renewable and storage zones, expanding transformer and cable manufacturing, and making large new loads more flexible. Data centers should increasingly be located where power and grid capacity already exist instead of forcing every region to build around them.

There is also value in preserving and upgrading existing firm generation. Keeping a safe nuclear plant open, improving an existing gas turbine or adding capacity to a hydro facility can be faster and less resource-intensive than building anything new. A speed-based strategy should be technologically pragmatic.

Yet it should also acknowledge what the construction market is saying. Renewables are not winning deployment simply because governments prefer them or because their emissions are lower. They are winning because factories can produce them continuously, developers can build them in parallel and investors can receive revenue sooner.

The electricity shortage is becoming a race against time. The technologies that can be deployed before the shortage peaks will shape the power system far more than those promising perfection after it has passed. Cheap power matters. Power delivered on time matters more.

text:
The Tesla Roadster was the first production car produced by the clean energy and electric vehicle company. Today, its best-selling nameplates are the affordable Model 3 sedan and Model Y small SUV.

Tesla's Roadster was a pricey performance-oriented enthusiast car designed to prove that EVs could be just as sporty (if not sportier) than iconic internal combustion engine performance vehicles.

Tesla is bringing back the Roadster, which will cost around $200,000, says MotorTrend. It costs $50,000 to reserve the new Roadster, according to the company's website. Is the $50,000 a worthy investment, or are there better performance EVs available within the same price range?

BMW's high-performance division is going electric

If I had $50,000 to put down on a new performance car with an electric powertrain, the 2026 BMW i4 M60 is one of the first models I'd look into. It starts at $70,700 before taxes and fees.

The BMW i4 M60 produces 563 horsepower and 586 pound-feet of torque. It rockets from 0-60 mph in 3.6 seconds, which is quick for its size. The i4 M60 has around 278 miles of driving range.

BMW offers plenty of packages to upgrade the i4 M60 including an M Carbo Exterior Package ($2,900). You can also add a Driving Assistance Professional Package ($1,700) for camera and radar based highway and city driving.

The 2026 BMW i4 M60 is a solid, more affordable Tesla Roadster alternative because the German luxury automaker is known for producing some of the best enthusiast vehicles money can buy. It's also quick and powerful.

The Porsche Taycan is mind-blowingly quick

I tested a Porsche Taycan for USA TODAY Cars and can confirm that the EV has superb handling and is a blast to drive. The Taycan comes in plenty of trims, but the Taycan Turbo model is the best trim to compete with the upcoming Tesla Roadster while still being more affordable.

The Porsche Taycan Turbo starts at $184,600. A $50,000 down payment on the Taycan would still amount to a substantial auto loan, but Porsche's electric car has the performance specs and driving dynamics to justify its price to some drivers.

Porsche's Taycan Turbo produces a whopping 871 horsepower. It zooms from 0-60 mph in 2.5 seconds. When it comes to electric performance vehicles, the Taycan is a top-tier model.

Lucid's electric car boasts excellent performance specs

The Lucid Air Grand Touring isn't as quick as the Porsche Taycan, but it's significantly cheaper than the Taycan and Tesla Roadster, while still putting up great performance numbers. The Lucid Air Grand Touring starts at $114,900 and produces 819 horsepower.

It goes from 0-60 mph in 3.0 seconds. The electric car has 480 miles of driving range, which is extremely practical.

Buyers can add the DreamDrive Pro package for $6,750. This package includes Advanced Driver Assistance Systems (ADAS) hardware that allows the vehicle to drive itself under supervision in certain scenarios.

I tested the Lucid Gravity SUV recently and enjoyed its futuristic software and features. The Lucid Air Grand Touring may not be as quick as other EVs, but it offers an ownership experience that's unique and convenient for drivers.

Tesla's new Roadster could set a new 0-60 time world record, but it's made for a very specific type of driver. If you aren't a die-hard Tesla fan willing to pay over $200,000 for a performance EV, it probably isn't worth reserving.

The Biden-era standards required certain coal-fired power plants and new natural gas plants to reduce their carbon dioxide emissions, including through carbon capture and storage technology.

text:
The Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) on Sept. 14 repealed most Biden-era carbon emissions standards for coal- and gas-fired power plants and proposed eliminating remaining federal greenhouse gas requirements for the power sector.

EPA Administrator Lee Zeldin announced the actions during a meeting of G20 energy ministers in Houston. The Biden-era standards required certain coal-fired power plants and new natural gas plants to reduce their carbon dioxide emissions, including through carbon capture and storage technology. Carbon capture and storage involves capturing carbon dioxide before it enters the atmosphere and storing it underground.

The EPA said the proposed repeal of the remaining standards would save the power industry $370 million in compliance costs over 20 years. Zeldin said the changes would make it easier to build generating capacity as electricity demand increases. Zeldin said, "That means cutting red tape so we can build new power-generating infrastructure."

The agency also proposed rescinding remaining greenhouse gas requirements for power plants based on its position that the Clean Air Act does not authorize the EPA to regulate the power sector's greenhouse gas emissions. That proposal would affect the legal basis for future federal carbon regulations covering power plants.

The EPA's actions remove most federal carbon requirements from a sector that accounts for nearly one-quarter of U.S. greenhouse gas emissions and propose eliminating the remaining requirements. The Biden administration estimated its power plant standards would prevent one billion metric tons of greenhouse gas emissions through 2047 and produce $370 billion in net benefits.

The repeal reduces federal compliance requirements for power companies, but state emissions rules will remain in effect. National Mining Association President and CEO Rich Nolan said the repeal "corrects the egregious misuse of the Clean Air Act as a political tool to end American coal generation and implements the law as Congress intended."

Environmental groups opposed the changes and said they would increase greenhouse gas emissions and associated health and environmental costs. Center for Biological Diversity Climate Law Institute attorney Maggie Coulter said, "Denying the existence of a quarter of the country's climate pollution is utterly reckless. It will lead to more lost lives and suffering from intense heatwaves, drastic storms and destructive wildfires, just like those we've seen this summer."

The Biden administration adopted the power plant carbon standards in 2024. The Trump administration proposed repealing them in June 2025 as part of a broader reconsideration of federal regulations covering fossil-fuel power plants.

President Donald Trump (R) and the EPA separately rescinded the 2009 endangerment finding in February 2026. The finding had concluded that greenhouse gases threaten public health and welfare and provided the legal foundation for federal greenhouse gas regulations covering motor vehicles. The administration also repealed federal vehicle greenhouse gas standards tied to that finding.

A coalition of 25 state attorneys general and other state and local officials sued the EPA in March 2026 to challenge the rescission. The plaintiffs argue the EPA's action violates the Clean Air Act and conflicts with U.S. Supreme Court precedent. The case remains pending in the U.S. Court of Appeals for the D.C. Circuit.

The EPA based that February action on its interpretation that the Clean Air Act does not authorize the agency to regulate greenhouse gases based on global climate effects. The Sept. 14 power-sector proposal would further limit the agency's authority to regulate greenhouse gas emissions from power plants.

New filings with the Georgia Public Service Commission outline how Google's subscription from proposed or planned nuclear uprates at Plants Hatch and Vogtle will benefit all customers

ATLANTA, Sept. 21, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Nuclear energy has long been an important part of Georgia's energy mix, with more than 25 percent of energy produced last year coming from nuclear, including the nation's largest generator of clean energy: Plant Vogtle near Waynesboro, Georgia. Today, Georgia Power and Google announced a new agreement that will further advance clean and reliable nuclear energy in the state while also providing significant savings for customers.

Under the agreement, which is subject to approval by the Georgia Public Service Commission (PSC), Google will support uprates on Georgia Power's owned portion of the nuclear units at Plants Vogtle and Hatch that will allow the facilities to add approximately 96 megawatts of new capacity to the electric grid to serve Georgia Power customers. Google's subscription is expected to enable approximately $900 million in projected benefits to customers over the life of the units.

The agreement is included in filings (Docket 44280, Docket 56002) made today at the Georgia PSC. The filings also include a new Nuclear Uprate (NU-1) tariff structure as well as a request to approve a new extended power uprate (EPU) for Plant Hatch 1 & 2. An EPU for Plant Vogtle 1 & 2 was previously approved by the Georgia PSC in the 2025 Integrated Resource Plan (IRP).

An EPU is a proven process that increases the electrical output of a nuclear generating unit through targeted modifications and upgrades to key plant equipment, such as turbines, pumps, motors, and cooling systems. These enhancements enable the reactor to operate at a higher licensed thermal power level, producing additional heat that increases steam flow to the turbine generator. As a result, the unit generates more electricity while continuing to utilize the existing reactor fuel design and plant infrastructure.

"Many of our large customers have specific clean energy goals, and we continue to work with the Georgia PSC to create programs that not only help them meet their goals, but align with our Customer Protection Pledge, enhancing the reliability and resiliency of the power grid and creating savings for all customers," said Aaron Mitchell, Senior Vice President of Strategic Growth for Georgia Power. "We appreciate Google's continued leadership in this space and partnership in developing this program, which we see as the latest example of how large-load growth can benefit all electric customers."

"Google data centers are long-term investments in the communities we call home, catalyzing local economic development and accelerating clean energy deployment. They also serve as a proof point for how we can unlock the significant opportunity to bring online new nuclear power through expanding the capacity of the existing nuclear fleet," said Lucia Tian, Director, Advanced Energy Technologies, Google. "This collaboration with Georgia Power ensures that digital infrastructure growth goes hand-in-hand with positive local impact, helping to deliver hundreds of millions of dollars in direct customer benefits and supporting a more affordable, clean, and reliable energy system for all Georgia residents."

The subscription-based program is an innovation on longstanding, successful renewable energy programs that Georgia Power has offered for years. As part of this transaction, Google will subscribe to the new NU-1 tariff and receive the Zero-Emission Credits (ZECs), which represent the carbon-free attributes of nuclear energy, associated with the power generated by the nuclear unit uprates. This structure, which also helps protect non-participating customers from incremental costs related to the uprate work, was originally contemplated as part of the 2025 IRP.

text:
AUSTIN, Texas (KTRK) -- Gov. Greg Abbott's office announced on Monday that the governor directed the Texas Commission on Environmental Quality (TCEQ) to halt all data center permits.

In a release, the governor's office said he directed the commission to halt permits until the Electric Reliability Council of Texas (ERCOT) completes its audit of data centers. According to the state officials, the audit is to ensure that the data centers' development "does not compromise the reliability of the Texas electric grid and does not put Texans’ natural resources at risk."

This announcement follows Abbott's previous announcement that he directed the Texas Water Development Board to penalize data centers that don't obey state water laws.

PREVIOUS REPORT: Gov. Greg Abbott calls for data center penalties if not complying with state water laws

The governor's office laid out guidelines for data center projects, stating that they must cover all their own electrical infrastructure costs, not use water needed by local communities, report electricity and water usage, and complete the ERCOT audit.

“Simply put, Texans must come first,” Governor Abbott stated in the release. “Data centers must pay their own way, protect our grid and water, and complete the ERCOT and TWDB audits. Until they do, TCEQ will issue no permits sought by data center projects.”

What: On September 17, 2026, the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) proposed a rule stating that it does not have the authority to regulate emissions from power plants in response to global climate change concerns.

Why: The EPA is proposing that Clean Air Act (CAA) Section 111 does not provide the agency with the authority to regulate greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions from power plants.

In a separate action published concurrently with this proposal, the EPA is finalizing the repeal of certain 2024 GHG standards for the fossil fuel-fired electric generating unit source category on distinct legal and technical grounds.

Specifically, the EPA asserts that that CAA section 111, the applicability and implications of the major questions doctrine, and the futility of power plant GHG standards in relation to the unique and global scale of the underlying problem similarly support the conclusion that the agency lacks authority to impose GHG regulations on power plants. The EPA also emphasizes the need for urgent action to avoid further expenditures in reliance on a potentially unlawful regulatory framework that may not further public health or welfare.

The EPA cites multiple Supreme Court decisions which clarify the limits of its authority in support of the proposal, including West Virginia v. EPA, Utility Air Regulatory Group v. EPA, Michigan v. EPA, and Loper Bright Enterprises v. Raimondo.

Should the EPA finalize its proposed conclusion that the Agency lacks statutory authority to regulate GHG emissions from power plants, that final action would remove the legal basis for all prior actions taken under CAA section 111 to regulate GHG emissions from these sources in response to global climate change.

The EPA identified 25 potentially affected small entities that would be impacted by the proposal. Under the repeal, the agency projects compliance cost savings of $6.8 million for these small entities in 2035 (this is the year with the highest projected cost savings). The EPA estimates no costs on small entities for the proposed rule.

The EPA will hold a virtual public hearing on the proposal on October 1, 2026.

By Hannah Pedone

SpaceX is one of a host of potential beneficiaries identified by Morgan Stanley as ways to play the intensifying AI power shortage

SpaceX made an intriguing acquisition that a Morgan Stanley analyst says sets the company up to benefit from a power crunch.

Amid skyrocketing demand for computing power and data-center capacity, the U.S. is facing a severe and growing power shortfall.

And a new analysis shows the electric grid may be even less equipped to handle the load than the industry previously thought. Data centers are becoming more efficient at providing computing power and moving more quickly than the grid can service.

Morgan Stanley analyst Stephen Byrd wrote in a Monday note that he expects a U.S. power shortfall of 33 gigawatts, which equates to 34% of chip demand, through 2028. Though that's excluding "time-to-power" solutions, like off-grid power, which bypass grid-connection delays.

But in the massive potential power shortfall lie ample opportunities for investors, according to Byrd.

One class of companies that stands to benefit from the crunch are powered shell providers, or companies that can repurpose their power grids to build data centers. He recommends Cipher Digital (CIFR), Hut 8 (HUT), Riot Platforms (RIOT), Galaxy Digital (GLXY) and Terawulf (WULF), saying that he expects each of these companies to sign at least one significant data-center lease within the next six months.

Freedom Capital Markets analyst Paul Meeks told MarketWatch that the supply-and-demand gap for power, while "already wide," could get "desperately worse" if power becomes even scarcer. And that scenario could boost the stocks of companies including Cipher Digital, Terawulf and Hut 8, which have secured power agreements for data centers, he noted.

Power-generation equipment is another compelling investment area, according to Byrd. He said he expects a "surge" in demand for products catering to "behind-the-meter" power generation, which allows energy-intensive facilities like data centers to store electricity on-site, as opposed to relying on the public grid.

Byrd recommends Bloom Energy (BE), GE Vernova (GEV) and Cummins (CMI). He expects there to be a number of "behind-the-meter" power generation deals in the coming months, especially in West Texas.

He also anticipates that companies involved in project development of behind-the-meter systems will see a flurry of transactions with data-center developers and AI companies. Those include Solaris Energy Infrastructure (SEI) and Vistra (VST).

SpaceX (SPCX) also stands to benefit from the power crunch for a little-known reason: its venture into gas turbines. Byrd pointed out that earlier this year, Elon Musk's company acquired the power provider APR Energy, which makes mobile gas turbines and power plants.

"SpaceX has a history of attacking whatever constrains scale most. As the company builds its moat in compute time and cost-to-power, it appears to have found its next target: turbine blades and vanes," he said, referring to gas turbine parts.

text:
The upcoming Batttery Show at Huntington Place in Detroit, October 12 through 15, will showcase developments in various battery technologies and issues. As expected, several sessions focus on advances in battery materials as engineers work to develop batteries with greater reliability and energy efficiency.

Here are some sessions attendees should find useful and informative. All the session times are Eastern.

Solid-State Batteries at the Crossroads: Promise vs. Production

https://tbsm26.mapyourshow.com/8_0/sessions/session-details.cfm?scheduleid=159

Tuesday, October 13, 1:00 PM - 1:15 PM, Room 140AB

Despite decades of research and investment, commercialization of solid-state batteries remains a challenge due to technical, economic, and scalability hurdles. This session will critically assess whether we are finally on the cusp of widespread solid-state battery adoption or whether semi-solid electrolytes will take over.

Key discussion points will include innovations in solid electrolytes, ranging from sulfides and polymers to halides, and their impact on conductivity and stability. We will also examine the integration of lithium-metal and silicon anodes, a key enabler for higher energy density, and the challenges related to dendrite formation and manufacturability. The session will also analyze how major industry players, including automakers and battery manufacturers, are investing in SSB technology and whether production costs and supply chain constraints could delay mass deployment.

The session will also explore market readiness, policy frameworks, and investment landscapes that could accelerate or hinder the commercialization of SSBs.

Beyond LFP: Where Does Sodium-Ion Fit in the Future Battery Mix?

https://tbsm26.mapyourshow.com/8_0/sessions/session-details.cfm?scheduleid=110

Tuesday, October 13, 3:50 PM - 4:10 PM Room 140AB

The development of solid-state batteries has largely focused on optimizing isolated material properties, such as electrolyte safety—often narrowly defined by non-flammability—or high ionic conductivity. However, this approach overlooks the coupled nature of electrochemical behaviors, where ion transport, interfacial contact, and electrode reactions collectively determine real-world performance and safety.

A critical misconception lies in equating non-flammable electrolytes with inherently safe batteries. In practice, safety risks are primarily governed by unstable electrode reactions and interfacial degradation, rather than electrolyte flammability alone. These unresolved electrochemical challenges at the cell level propagate into system-level penalties, including increased structural complexity, added weight, and higher manufacturing costs. Material reactivity and process sensitivity further hinder scalability.

In this talk, Vincent Yang of Prologium Technology discusses a Solid-State Battery 2.0 platform that shifts from single-parameter optimization to a chemistry-integrated design framework. By simultaneously stabilizing electrode reactions, enabling robust interfacial transport without external pressure, and simplifying material and process requirements, this approach addresses both performance and safety at their origins.

The Pressure Problem in Solid-State Batteries: Engineering for Performance, Durability & Scale

https://tbsm26.mapyourshow.com/8_0/sessions/session-details.cfm?scheduleid=114

Wednesday, October 14, 4:10 PM - 4:30 PM, Room 140AB

Solid‑state battery systems introduce new challenges for mechanical pressure management compared to traditional pouch and prismatic lithium‑ion cells. Conventional elastomeric pads—commonly used to provide low, compliant counterforce during cell breathing—are designed to compress easily while accommodating long‑term cell expansion from mechanisms such as dendrite formation or gas generation.

However, solid‑state chemistries require substantially higher installation pressures, typically 1–3 MPa at beginning‑of‑life, and they experience greater dimensional changes during cycling. While silicone and polyurethane pad materials can achieve these higher counterforces, they generally must be implemented at significantly increased thickness to absorb the larger expansion profiles, which can create packaging and design constraints.

To address these limitations, Rogers is developing differentiated pressure‑management materials engineered to deliver the required force levels for solid‑state cells while maintaining more conventional pad thicknesses, improving both performance and pack‑level integration. Rogers will discuss these materials in a lightning talk

The Best Electrode Is No Electrode: Anode-Free Sodium Batteries

https://tbsm26.mapyourshow.com/8_0/sessions/session-details.cfm?scheduleid=98

Tuesday, October 13, 3:30 PM - 3:50 PM Room 140AB

This talk, given by a former Tesla engineer who has launched a sodium-ion company, will explore how “innovation by subtraction” can be applied to sodium-ion battery chemistry in an anode-free cell design, resulting in the lowest bill-of-materials available.

Scaling Advanced Materials from R&D to Commercial Production

https://tbsm26.mapyourshow.com/8_0/sessions/session-details.cfm?scheduleid=305

Thursday, October 15, 11:00 AM - 11:30 AM Room 140AB

This session examines the challenges of moving advanced battery materials from laboratory research to reliable, cost-effective commercial production. It will explore scale-up, process control, quality consistency, supply availability, qualification timelines, and manufacturing integration required to bring new materials successfully to market.

title: EPA Withdraws PFAS Guidance as North Carolina Battles Water Contamination
description:
This guidance was supposed to stop PFAS from getting into drinking water sources, rivers, and towns.
The withdrawal arrives as North Carolina grapples with widespread contamination problems across the state.
Big chemical manufacturers such as 3M and Chemours are known as the biggest producers of PFAS in North Carolina.
State officials in North Carolina slammed the proposal as a backroom deal reached through negotiations in which they were not included.
North Carolina does not have its own state-enforceable regulations on PFAS in public drinking water yet.
text:
The Environmental Protection Agency pulled guidance that pushed states and wastewater utilities to use Clean Water Act powers against PFAS pollution, according to WWAY TV. This guidance was supposed to stop PFAS from getting into drinking water sources, rivers, and towns.

Assistant administrator for the Office of Water Jessica Kramer signed a memo. That memo led to the removal of the guidance from the agency's website. The Southern Environmental Law Center blasted the decision, arguing the guidance helped states and utilities fight PFAS pollution where it starts.

PFAS are man-made chemicals. They include PFOA, PFOS, and GenX. These chemicals stick around in the environment for decades and have been connected with cancer, weakened immune systems, developmental delays, and infertility.

The withdrawal arrives as North Carolina grapples with widespread contamination problems across the state. Water sources like the Haw River and Jordan Lake provide drinking water to almost one million residents, but they've dealt with decades of pollution from runoff and discharge operations at manufacturing sites and military bases nearby.

Big chemical manufacturers such as 3M and Chemours are known as the biggest producers of PFAS in North Carolina. A 2024 test of an elementary school's well in Asheboro discovered contamination at amounts 233 times over federal safety standards.

In June, the agency and the U.S. Department of Justice announced a $450 million settlement with Chemours. The settlement would require the manufacturer to pay out $22.5 million in civil penalties for alleged toxic waste violations in North Carolina, West Virginia, and New Jersey. State officials in North Carolina slammed the proposal as a backroom deal reached through negotiations in which they were not included.

The withdrawal does not change existing legal requirements under the Clean Water Act. States and wastewater treatment plants can still use the law to control PFAS discharges before they reach sewage sludge, farmland, rivers, and drinking water supplies.

North Carolina does not have its own state-enforceable regulations on PFAS in public drinking water yet. In 2024, the state's Environmental Management Commission rejected a proposed set of rules backed by years of public health research.

"These rules have no teeth to actually protect us," said Dr. Kelly McConnell, a pediatrician and chair of the Sierra Club's chapter in southeastern North Carolina, according to The Progressive. "These companies can continue dumping and nothing will happen to them."

According to The Progressive, installing specialized filters at a water treatment plant cost the Cape Fear Public Utility Authority almost $50 million in 2022.

text:
A majority of the North Carolina Utilities Commission pointed to concerns about timing and whether data centers would bear enough of the cost in taking the rare step of denying Duke Energy a key regulatory approval for a new gas plant.

Duke was asking the commission for a certificate of public convenience and necessity to build a new combustion turbine at its Sherwood H. Smith Jr. Energy Complex near Hamlet, a Richmond County town near the South Carolina border. The proposed plant would also be close to Amazon's under-construction $10 billion data center, and questions about how much of its power would be used for data center projects played a major role in commissioners' skepticism.

The commissioners found that Duke failed to prove that the new turbine is necessary in part because Utilities Commission staff has not yet vetted Duke's modeled load growth — of which about 70% comes from data centers — as part of its ongoing 2025 Carbon Plan and Integrated Resource Plan case.

Beyond that, commissioners found that Duke hadn't discussed how much of the power from the anticipated $584 million turbine would be used to power data centers and, to the extent it would be, how those customers would pay for the project. Duke needed to better demonstrate, commissioners found, how it would comply with the White House Ratepayer Protection Pledge the utility signed onto earlier this year.

"The application for a CPCN is premature and the record is consequently insufficient for the Commission to determine whether the proposed facility satisfies all the applicable requirements for issuance of a CPCN," commissioners wrote in their order.

Commissioners voting to deny the certificate included Bill Brawley, Tommy Tucker and Donald van der Vaart - all Republican appointees. Commissioner Floyd McKissick, a Democrat,

voted to grant it and wrote a dissenting opinion. Commissioner John Gadja did not vote.

It is exceptionally rare for the Utilities Commission to deny Duke Energy a certificate of public convenience and necessity.

"I think that unprecedented wouldn’t be too strong a word to use here. You know, CPCNs have generally been sort of a formality in recent years, and I think it just shows how skeptical the Commission is of putting these costs on ratepayers," Will Scott, the Environmental Defense Fund's North Carolina policy director, said in an interview.

In a concurring opinion, Tucker wrote specifically to the concerns about how much of the turbine's electricity would go to data centers. While witnesses said the turbine wasn't being built for a specific project, he wrote, it was not lost on him that it is very close to the proposed Amazon facility and that the Utilities Commission had approved a new transmission line to that facility.

"(Duke) should provide additional evidence regarding the extent to which the Proposed Facility is needed to provide service to data centers, and how much those data centers will contribute to costs," Tucker wrote.

Duke Energy's stance

Duke's Smith Complex already features a pair of combined cycle gas plants that can generate 1.08 gigawatts of power, as well as five combustion turbines that can generate up to an additional 820 megawatts.

Combined cycle plants are typically used to generate baseload electricity, or the power that is needed from day to day, while combustion turbines are often referred to as "peakers" because they are used when electricity demand peaks.

For example, Duke modeled the proposed turbine's use in 10 years with typical weather. It found that the turbine would be used more than 10% of the time in four of those years.

Craig Wilson, a Duke Energy spokesman, wrote that the company is reviewing the commission's decision and considering its next steps.

"We believe we have demonstrated that the Smith CT is part of a least-cost path to maintain reliable and affordable service for customers as energy demand continues to grow across North Carolina," Wilson wrote.

During evidentiary hearings, Duke officials told the commission that because Smith was configured for a sixth turbine, it could be built and start generating power relatively quickly. They were hoping to have the new turbine operating by 2030.

Duke witnesses also warned commissioners that not granting the certificate might not only delay the in-service date of the turbine, but also potentially result in higher construction costs.

McKissick's dissenting opinion called the decision to deny the certificate "a serious error of judgment," focusing in part on how much it would cost to build the turbine.

Failing to move forward with the project now would likely result in higher costs to ratepayers if Duke seeks approval in the future, McKissick wrote. He noted that in rebuttal testimony, a Duke witness said the utility had received two bids that were much lower than the initial estimates.

"Ratepayers should not be required to bear the costs of delay resulting from the denial of a facility which the record plainly demonstrates is needed," McKissick wrote.

McKissick also wrote that there is no other plan that can add firm power to Duke's energy mix like the proposed turbine.

Are there other options?

Public Staff, the state agency that represents the interest of ratepayers in utility cases, also recommended that the Utilities Commission approve the new turbine despite what it called a "staggering" $584 million price tag.

During the evidentiary hearing, Dustin Metz, a Public Staff engineer, said he would recommend moving forward with the project despite that price tag because of concerns Duke's ability to reliably provide power to a growing state in coming years.

"Because Duke hasn't put forward an alternative that actually can be implemented in a timeline to mitigate that reliability concern that we're seeing, we are now, for lack of a better word, stuck with this resource," Metz said.

But commissioners disagreed, pointing to 2025's Senate Bill 266, which among other things tweaked the state's utilities laws to say the commission can grant a certificate of public convenience and necessity only after comparing the cost of a proposed facility to other resources like grid modernization, storage, energy efficiency and demand-side management, among others.

In his concurring opinion, van der Vaart wrote that Duke had failed to make those comparisons. While some kind of dispatchable resources may be necessary by 2030, van der Vaart wrote, the record did not prove that the turbine was the least-expensive way of meeting that need as required under SB 266.

"The record should allow the Commission to evaluate the alternatives, their costs, their reliability attributes, their limitations, and the reasons they cannot establish or maintain a more cost-effective and reliable system. An assertion that the Proposed Facility is the only resource that can be completed in time does not by itself substitute for that analysis," van der Vaart wrote.

Commissioners left open the possibility that Duke can better address the concerns they raised and re-file the application.

title: Governor Abbott Directs TCEQ To Halt Data Center Permits
description:
Governor Greg Abbott today directed the Texas Commission on Environmental Quality (TCEQ) to halt all permits sought by data centers until the Electric Reliability Council of Texas (ERCOT) completes its audit.
“Simply put, Texans must come first,” said Governor Abbott.
“Data centers must pay their own way, protect our grid and water, and complete the ERCOT and TWDB audits.
Data center projects must cover all electrical infrastructure costs, result in lower residential electrical bills, and complete the ERCOT audit.
Next session, Governor Abbott will work with the Legislature to eliminate any financial incentives for data centers.
text:
Governor Greg Abbott today directed the Texas Commission on Environmental Quality (TCEQ) to halt all permits sought by data centers until the Electric Reliability Council of Texas (ERCOT) completes its audit. Because the Public Utility Commission of Texas (PUCT), ERCOT, and the Texas Water Development Board (TWDB) require that information to make informed decisions, no state agency shall move forward with regulatory approvals related to data center development until it is acquired.

“Simply put, Texans must come first,” said Governor Abbott. “Data centers must pay their own way, protect our grid and water, and complete the ERCOT and TWDB audits. Until they do, TCEQ will issue no permits sought by data center projects.”

Governor Abbott directed the PUCT and ERCOT to audit all data centers undergoing ERCOT’s interconnection process so their development does not compromise the reliability of the Texas electric grid and does not put Texans’ natural resources at risk. On September 14, he directed TWDB to compel data centers to comply with water-use reporting requirements, impose legal consequences for past and future failure to comply with state law, and partner with ERCOT on the audit to obtain additional water-use information. The PUCT, ERCOT, and TWDB will determine the impact of data centers on grid reliability and security and on the water resources needed by Texas communities.

Data center projects must cover all electrical infrastructure costs, result in lower residential electrical bills, and complete the ERCOT audit. Data centers must not use water needed by local communities, must report electricity and water usage, and must abide by setback requirements that will protect the communities in which they operate.

As ERCOT and TWDB conduct their audits, TCEQ must align its permitting decisions with the Governor’s directives and use the information from those audits. TCEQ shall provide an update to the Office of the Governor on its compliance with this directive by Monday, October 19, 2026.

Next session, Governor Abbott will work with the Legislature to eliminate any financial incentives for data centers.

title: LFP Cathode Materials to Surge to 5.24 Million Tons This Year, Commanding 77% of Total Market
description:
China Accelerates Transition to High-Density LFP Production expansion is even steeper in China, the world's largest LFP producer.
China's LFP production in the first half of this year reached approximately 2.7 million tons, up 73% year-over-year.
Prismatic Batteries Dominate the ESS Market The dominance of prismatic batteries in the ESS battery market is expected to strengthen further.
ESS Market to Enter the 1,000 GWh Era Next Year The growth trajectory of the ESS battery market is expected to continue for the foreseeable future.
With Chinese manufacturers dominating the market through LFP battery price competitiveness, South Korean companies are seeking business expansion opportunities in the U.S. market.
text:
Lithium iron phosphate (LFP) cathode materials have established themselves as the dominant force in the battery cathode materials market, riding surging demand from entry-level electric vehicles and energy storage systems (ESS). Global LFP cathode material shipments are projected to reach 5.24 million tons this year, up 51% from last year, with their share of the total lithium-ion battery cathode materials market expanding to 77%.

According to data released by market research firm SNE Research on the 21st, LFP's market dominance has risen sharply in recent years. In 2024, LFP accounted for 2.36 million tons, or 64%, of the 3.7 million tons of global cathode material shipments. Last year, that figure climbed to 3.47 million tons, pushing the share to 72%. In the first half of this year, LFP shipments grew 73% year-over-year, expanding the share to 76%.

Two factors are driving LFP growth. First is demand for entry-level EVs, which leverage LFP's price competitiveness, thermal safety, and long cycle life. While LFP has lower energy density than nickel-cobalt-based ternary cathode materials, its lower cost burden and reduced fire risk have accelerated adoption, particularly in entry-level EVs and commercial vehicles.

Second is the explosive growth of the ESS market. As AI data center power demand surges and renewable energy expansion increases the need for large-scale power storage, ESS has emerged as a new growth engine for LFP. Global ESS battery shipments reached 461.3 gigawatt-hours (GWh) in the first half of this year, up 71% year-over-year. The North American market grew 83% to 75.9 GWh, demonstrating that LFP demand is rapidly expanding beyond China.

China Accelerates Transition to High-Density LFP

Production expansion is even steeper in China, the world's largest LFP producer. China's LFP production in the first half of this year reached approximately 2.7 million tons, up 73% year-over-year. SNE Research estimates that average capacity utilization among Chinese LFP manufacturers has exceeded 80%, with some leading players approaching full-capacity operation.

However, with oversupply persisting in commodity-grade products, the competitive focus is shifting toward high-density, high-performance materials. Major Chinese manufacturers are moving their center of gravity from third-generation and earlier products to 3.5- to 4th-generation and above high-density LFP production. Recently, development of high-density LFP with compression density above 2.6 g/cc has emerged as a key direction, and competition in lithium manganese iron phosphate (LMFP), which has the potential to boost energy density by approximately 15-20% over LFP, is also intensifying.

Korean Battery Makers Accelerate North American ESS Market Push

South Korean battery makers are also moving quickly to build LFP production and supply chains targeting the rapidly growing North American ESS market.

South Korea's LG Energy Solution (373220.KS) began full operations at its Lansing, Michigan plant last month. The facility is a multi-purpose hub targeting annual production capacity of over 35 GWh, producing both LFP batteries for ESS and nickel-cobalt-manganese (NCM) batteries for EVs. The company has established five ESS production bases in North America, including the Lansing plant, to respond to growing local demand.

South Korea's Samsung SDI (006400.KS) plans to begin mass production of LFP batteries for ESS at its StarPlus Energy (SPE) plant in Indiana in the fourth quarter of this year. To secure its cathode material supply chain, the company signed a supply agreement with L&F worth approximately ₩1.6 trillion (approximately $1.2 billion) over three years starting next year. The strategy aims to connect North American production facilities with South Korean materials companies to secure a stable LFP supply chain for ESS.

South Korea's SK On also signed a supply agreement this month with L&F for high-density third-generation LFP cathode materials worth approximately ₩160 billion (approximately $116.0 million) through 2028. The company has been expanding its related business, having previously signed a 9 GWh ESS LFP battery supply agreement with U.S.-based Neovolta Power.

Prismatic Batteries Dominate the ESS Market

The dominance of prismatic batteries in the ESS battery market is expected to strengthen further. Prismatic batteries are estimated to account for 94% of the global ESS battery market this year. The share is expected to dip slightly to 92% next year before rising again from 2028, reaching 97% by 2035.

The temporary decline in prismatic share next year is attributed to increased pouch-type supply targeting the U.S. market. Industry sources explain that LG Energy Solution's production of pouch cells for the U.S. market will expand the pouch-type share next year compared to this year. However, the pouch cell share is expected to gradually decline thereafter.

Prismatic batteries' high market share aligns with the characteristics of ESS, which requires stable operation of large-capacity batteries. Prismatic cells are encased in rigid aluminum cans, providing structural rigidity, and it is relatively easier to scale cell sizes to meet required capacities. In contrast, pouch-type batteries offer advantages in energy density and space utilization but require structural reinforcement due to their thin film exterior, and safety design burdens increase as cells grow larger. Cylindrical batteries also face thermal management challenges during scaling, as larger diameters make it more difficult to dissipate internal heat.

South Korea's battery industry is also focusing on securing prismatic competitiveness. Samsung SDI has produced prismatic batteries as its mainstay since 2009. LG Energy Solution and SK On, which built their businesses primarily around pouch-type batteries, are also accelerating expansion into prismatic product lines.

ESS Market to Enter the 1,000 GWh Era Next Year

The growth trajectory of the ESS battery market is expected to continue for the foreseeable future. Annual ESS battery shipments are projected to rise from 984 GWh this year to 1,150 GWh next year, surpassing 1,000 GWh for the first time. Growth is expected to continue thereafter, reaching 1,870 GWh by 2035—approximately double this year's level.

The key challenge is converting ESS demand expansion into actual orders and market share gains. With Chinese manufacturers dominating the market through LFP battery price competitiveness, South Korean companies are seeking business expansion opportunities in the U.S. market. Industry assessments note that while Chinese battery makers have captured the market through low-price LFP strategies, South Korean battery makers are now pursuing a resurgence in the U.S. market based on prismatic technology.

The LFP market is expected to maintain its growth trajectory centered on entry-level EVs and ESS. However, large-scale capacity expansion by Chinese manufacturers is likely to intensify oversupply and price competition in commodity-grade products. South Korea's three major battery makers must differentiate beyond simply increasing LFP production volume, focusing on high density, fast charging, and low-temperature performance. Securing ESS demand for AI data centers and power grids, backed by North American local production and supply chains, will determine the success or failure of their LFP businesses going forward.

title: EPA Repeals Carbon Standards for Power Plants - Chapman and Cutler LLP
description:
The EPA supplemented its repeal with a proposal to rescind the remaining standards by repealing its Greenhouse Gas Standards for Fossil Fuel-Fired Power Plants and Regulations for Power Plant Greenhouse Gas Emissions under Clean Air Act Section 111.
In 2024, the Biden Administration finalized a rule that set standards under the Clean Air Act to reduce greenhouse gas emissions from new gas plants and existing coal-fired power plants.
Among other things, the standards required the use of carbon capture and sequestration technology on coal-fired power plants operating past 2039 and on modified or reconstructed units.
The 2024 carbon pollution standards represented a second attempt to regulate greenhouse gas emissions from fossil fuel-fired power plants.
Environmental and public health groups have already filed lawsuits against the EPA challenging its repeal of the 2024 carbon pollution standards.
text:
Client Alert

On September 14, 2026, the Environmental Protection Agency (“EPA”) issued a final rule that repealed substantially all of the carbon pollution standards set in 2024 with respect to fossil fuel-fired power plants. The EPA supplemented its repeal with a proposal to rescind the remaining standards by repealing its Greenhouse Gas Standards for Fossil Fuel-Fired Power Plants and Regulations for Power Plant Greenhouse Gas Emissions under Clean Air Act Section 111.

Background and Rescission

The EPA forecasted this move when, in February 2026, it rescinded its Greenhouse Gas Endangerment Finding and subsequent federal greenhouse gas emission standards for cars and trucks. The EPA asserts that its actions will ensure “affordable and reliable energy supplies and drive down costs of transportation, heating, utilities, farming, and manufacturing while boosting our national security.” The EPA estimates that the final rule will save the power sector up to $310 billion in compliance costs.

In 2024, the Biden Administration finalized a rule that set standards under the Clean Air Act to reduce greenhouse gas emissions from new gas plants and existing coal-fired power plants. Among other things, the standards required the use of carbon capture and sequestration technology on coal-fired power plants operating past 2039 and on modified or reconstructed units. The 2024 carbon pollution standards represented a second attempt to regulate greenhouse gas emissions from fossil fuel-fired power plants. The Obama Administration issued the Clean Power Plan in 2015, which aimed to cut greenhouse gas emissions by 870 million tons by 2030. The Clean Power Plan was subsequently struck down by the Supreme Court.

Environmental and public health groups have already filed lawsuits against the EPA challenging its repeal of the 2024 carbon pollution standards. Additional lawsuits are expected to follow.

The Solar For All program provides grant funding to regions across the country in order to expand affordable solar energy to over 900,000 households. Last summer, Donald Trump’s Environmental Protection Agency announced it would rescind the funds and ended the program.

Solar energy is one of the cheapest forms of energy, and in June 2026, solar production in the U.S. overtook coal production for the first month on record. Despite the administration’s attempts to cut funding and end projects, renewable energy has continued to grow in popularity and production in the country.

In response, Sierra Club Climate Policy Director Patrick Drupp issued the following statement:

“Solar energy is cheap, reliable, and quick to get online. It is a common sense solution to address the record-high electricity bills that families are seeing, while improving public health and cleaning up our air and water. We are glad to see the courts agree with Sierra Club that the administration’s attempt to end the Solar For All program is unlawful, and we will continue to defend this program to ensure families everywhere can reap the benefits of solar energy.”

Matthew Chen, External Affairs Manager, North America, ABB E-mobility Inc. and Electric Vehicle Charging Association Chair:“ Meeting California’s clean transportation goals means building more than 400 new chargers a day, every day, through 2030. Laura Renger, Executive Director, California Electric Transportation Coalition: “Thank you, Governor Newsom, for signing SB 1213 and SB 1283 today. These bills are good news for California’s electric-transportation future, bringing greater transparency to zero-emission incentives for medium- and heavy-duty vehicles while making it easier to build the charging infrastructure Californians need. CalETC applauds the Governor and bill authors for clearing unnecessary barriers and keeping California moving forward.”

Bill Mcgavern, Policy Director, Coalition for Clean Air: “Electrifying transportation is an essential tool for cleaning up California’s air, fighting catastrophic climate change, and creating quality jobs. These new laws will help build the infrastructure to enable all Californians — including residents of multi-family housing — to benefit from clean electric mobility. In addition, price transparency requirements will help build a more affordable market for the zero-emission trucks we need to reduce the toxic diesel exhaust poisoning our communities.”

Guillermo Ortiz, Senior Clean Vehicle Advocate, Natural Resources Defense Council: “The transition to clean vehicles is a smart business move, not a financial burden. By bringing transparency to the marketplace and enhancing our voucher programs, this bipartisan legislation will drive down costs, protect our small businesses from fuel price volatility, expedite EV charging and ensure California remains a leader in both environmental and economic innovation.”

Daniel Barrad, Western States Associate Director, Union of Concerned Scientists: “As the Trump administration rolls back life-saving policies and raises costs, California’s progress on zero emission transportation is more important than ever. We applaud the legislature and governor for enacting laws that will advance clean, affordable and sustainable transportation. From increasing charging access to laying the groundwork for battery recycling, these laws show the world that a safe, clean and reliable transportation future is possible.”

Gracyna Mohabir, Sr. Regulatory Advocate, California Environmental Voters: “Transportation is California’s largest source of pollution and a major contributor to the state’s poor air quality. At a time when the federal government is systematically dismantling our clean air and health protections, this is an important step toward building a cleaner freight future. “We need practical solutions that make it easier to choose zero-emissions vehicles and create a freight system that doesn’t come at the expense of Californians’ health and clean air, and SB 1213 is exactly that.”

Jakob Evans, Senior Policy Strategist, Sierra Club California: “Signing this package of bills shows that California is stepping up to lead on clean air at a time when the federal government has undermined the electric vehicle market and attacked our state’s regulatory autonomy. Bills like SB 1213 will ensure that California is able to take more effective action to accelerate deployment of zero-emission trucks and address our largest sector of pollution. Sierra Club California will continue to work closely with state leaders to fight for California’s air quality and public health.”

California’s clean transportation leadership

The legislation signed today builds on the Governor’s MyFirstEV program, which is helping first-time zero-emission vehicle buyers access immediate savings on their first electric vehicle purchase. Through MyFirstEV, eligible Californians can receive an instant rebate of up to $3,500 toward a qualifying new zero-emission vehicle or up to $1,750 toward a qualifying used vehicle.

California’s $600 million investment in an affordable clean-vehicle future includes programs that help income-qualified residents replace older, higher-polluting cars; support fleets in purchasing cleaner trucks and buses; and replace high-polluting engines and equipment.

The Golden State has more than 216,445 public and shared charging plugs statewide, including more than 20,000 DC fast-charging ports. Chargers are being installed at places Californians already go, including workplaces, multifamily housing, retail centers, park-and-ride lots, medical offices, and travel corridors.

The California Energy Commission allocated $98.5 million in light-duty ZEV infrastructure funding for fiscal year 2025-26, emphasizing Level 1 and Level 2 chargers in locations where cars are parked for longer periods, including homes and multifamily residences.

California is one of the top states for EV buyers and drivers. California has surpassed its original goal of 1.5 million zero-emission vehicle sales by 2025, reaching more than 2.7 million cumulative ZEV sales. In the second quarter of 2026, Californians purchased 86,857 new ZEVs, representing 19.1% of all new vehicle sales in the state.

text:
Key takeaways

Amazon’s carbon-free energy projects contributed nearly $11 billion to U.S. GDP from 2023 through 2025.

These investments supported nearly 22,000 jobs annually across the country.

Amazon covers all costs associated with powering its data centers, so communities benefit from these investments without bearing expenses.

Amazon's carbon-free energy projects don't just keep the lights on for our operations—they put people to work, support tax revenue generation into local communities, and drive economic growth.

A new independent study by Oxford Economics puts a number on it: Amazon's carbon-free energy investments contributed nearly $11 billion to United States gross domestic product (GDP) and supported nearly 22,000 jobs annually from 2023 through 2025. That’s across our full portfolio of carbon-free energy projects—including solar farms, wind farms, nuclear energy, and battery storage systems.

What happens when Amazon invests in carbon-free energy?

Amazon's carbon-free energy portfolio spans more than 700 projects across 28 countries, totaling more than 40 gigawatts (GW) of capacity—enough to power more than 12.1 million U.S. homes.

Every project creates jobs in layers. Construction crews, welders, and electricians build the project, while local vendors, suppliers, and logistics companies support the building. Those paychecks get spent at nearby restaurants, shops, and service businesses. After construction wraps, plant managers, maintenance teams, and technical specialists keep things running for decades. Oxford Economics found these projects enabled billions in estimated tax revenue from 2023 through 2025—money that increases public funds to support schools, roads, first responders, and public services in the communities where they operate.

“Investment in America’s energy infrastructure has benefits that extend well beyond the electricity it generates,” said Pete Collings, managing director of economic footprint and sustainability at Oxford Economics. “Amazon's purchases of carbon-free power support jobs and economic activity across the country, stimulate tax revenues that can pay for public services, and contribute to a more secure and resilient energy system.”

These projects last anywhere from 25 to 60 years depending on the technology. Oxford Economics estimates that through 2034 alone, the total contribution will top $61 billion in GDP while supporting roughly 23,500 jobs annually.

How do these projects benefit local communities?

Mississippi

In Tunica County, Mississippi, Amazon's Delta Wind project is the first utility-scale wind farm in the state. Developed by AES and operational since April 2024, the 184.5-megawatt project generates enough carbon-free energy to power the equivalent of nearly 80,000 Mississippi homes a year. Landowners continue to farm the acreage around the turbines, preserving the county's agricultural heritage alongside its new energy infrastructure.

“These are powerful examples of how we're not only providing the carbon-free energy that companies like Amazon need to grow, but helping states like Mississippi attract critical investment, create new sources of revenue for landowners and local communities, and support sustainable economic growth for decades to come,” said Amanda Smith, vice president of external affairs, U.S. renewables and power, at AES.

Statewide, Amazon's carbon-free energy projects contributed $212 million to Mississippi's GDP from 2023 through 2025, supporting approximately 280 jobs annually and enabling more than $22 million in tax revenue.

The benefits extend to everyday ratepayers as well. Entergy Mississippi reports that revenue from large customers like data centers is beginning to deliver direct benefits, helping keep electricity rates flat through the peak summer months. Through its Fair Share Plus Pledge, the utility projects more than $2 billion in savings for Mississippi customers over the next two decades and has credited large-customer revenue with supporting reliability improvements across its system.

Virginia

Amazon's carbon-free energy projects in Virginia contributed more than $331 million to the state's GDP from 2023 through 2025, supporting more than 150 jobs annually and enabling over $15 million in tax revenue.

The benefits also reach communities in more direct ways. In Louisa County, Amazon awarded a $135,000 grant to fully fund a solar project for the Louisa County Resource Council (LCRC), the county's primary source of free food for nearly 4,000 residents each month. The new solar system is expected to cut roughly $1,000 from LCRC's monthly utility bill, savings it estimates could put nearly 48,000 meals on its clients' tables each year.

Indiana

In Indiana, Amazon has worked alongside local leaders who see firsthand how our carbon-free energy projects translate into jobs, new sources of tax revenue, and long-term economic development for their communities.

“What's exciting for our region is the ripple effect. While we see Amazon’s investment in data centers, we also understand what their investment across the state has enabled in carbon-free energy (CFE),” said Jeff Rea, president and CEO of South Bend Regional Chamber. “We're proud to have a company investing in the South Bend Region which pushes beyond its project boundaries to support Hoosiers across the state.”

Statewide, investments made by developers for Amazon's carbon-free energy projects contributed $160 million to Indiana's GDP from 2023 through 2025, supporting approximately 116 jobs annually and enabling more than $11 million in tax revenue.

Texas

Amazon's carbon-free energy portfolio in Texas is the largest of any state, with more than 10 gigawatts of capacity across solar, wind, and nuclear projects—enough to power approximately 8 million U.S. homes. From 2023 through 2025, Amazon’s carbon-free energy projects contributed over $1 billion to the state's GDP, supported over 1,300 jobs annually, and enabled over $143 million in tax revenue across the state.

“Corporate commitments to carbon-free energy are strengthening Texas's reputation as a great place to do business,” said Bryn Baker of the Texas Energy Buyers Alliance. “Amazon alone has 10 gigawatts of carbon emissions-free energy capacity in the state, spanning solar, wind, and nuclear. Large energy customers want to grow their operations in the Lone Star State, and they are ready and willing to invest in the low-cost, reliable, carbon-free energy resources that can support that growth.”

What's the future for Amazon's carbon-free energy portfolio?

Amazon builds the energy it needs in ways that also benefit surrounding communities—with sources that will last for decades. As we work toward our Climate Pledge goal of net-zero carbon by 2040, every carbon-free energy project we bring online gets us closer and leaves the local economy stronger in the process.

text:
Current pipeline monitors detect leaks without identifying the escaping gas, creating a blind spot that can delay emergency responses and endanger communities.

A new LSU system uses unique fiber-optic sensor coatings to tell the difference between carbon dioxide, nitrogen, methane and ordinary air flow, as well as humidity. The sensors could slash millions from monitoring, repairs and leak prevention costs.

“The gas identity tells you what danger you face. Humidity tells you how the danger will behave and how fast the pipeline may deteriorate,” said FNU Jyoti, a postdoctoral research associate in the Department of Petroleum Engineering.

CO₂ displaces oxygen, can pool in low-lying areas, suffocate people and animals and make metal pipes brittle. Add moisture, and CO₂ can form carbonic acid, accelerating corrosion that could lead to catastrophic pipeline failure.

The research team lab-tested its system but mixed in humidity to simulate field conditions.

“Moisture can influence sensor performance. We wanted to analyze how humidity affects our CO₂ sensing response to reduce the threat of carbonic acid formation,” Jyoti said.

The research team includes LSU Petroleum Engineering Associate Professor Jyotsna Sharma, LSU Mechanical and Industrial Engineering Associate Professor Manas Ranjan Gartia, Jyoti and Satyendra Kumar Mishra, a senior researcher at the Centre Tecnològic de Telecomunicacions de Catalunya in Spain.

The new monitoring system builds on Sharma’s earlier work using fiber-optic sensors to track leaks by measuring physical changes inside a pipeline, such as temperature, pressure and stress. However, external or environmental conditions, like temperature or traffic vibration, can compromise those measurements.

The researchers coated the fiber with metal-organic frameworks (MOFs), porous hybrid materials whose development was recognized with the 2025 Nobel Prize in Chemistry.

MOFs’ crystalline structures form precisely sized pores just nanometers wide. The pores can grab and hold specific molecules. The research team tailored MOF coatings to detect individual gases.

The team also built a numerical model that predicts MOF performance with more than 95% accuracy. Researchers can digitally screen dozens of potential materials before moving to lab testing, saving months of work.

After lab testing, the researchers’ next step will be large-scale experiments in a 5,000-foot wellbore.

“Our goal is to show there is a clear path from our research prototype to a real-world solution,” Jyoti said.

The research team is working with the LSU Office of Innovation & Technology Commercialization to find partners or funding to advance the leak detection system.

“This pipeline safety breakthrough illustrates how LSU is advancing toward our goal of becoming a Top 50 research institution,” said Robert Twilley, vice chancellor of research and economic development. “By turning research into practical solutions, our scientists are tackling global energy challenges head-on, protecting communities and saving industry millions of dollars.”

text:
Two months after Louisiana became a finalist for a national initiative to modernize nuclear power, state officials have begun meeting with local officials — most recently in East and West Feliciana parishes — about interest in new nuclear development.

Such companies could include those engaged in recycling spent radioactive fuel rods, nuclear fuel enrichment and permanently storing nuclear waste.

The state Department of Conservation and Energy, which is leading Louisiana’s effort to win the federal competition, met with local officials last week in south Louisiana and will hit the northern part of the state soon.

“We’re visiting different areas saying, ‘Hey, here’s the kind of things that are out there that might be part of it. Is there anything you’ve got an interest in?’” said Patrick Courreges, a state energy department spokesman.

One such meeting took place with East Feliciana officials late last week, said Police Juror Richard Oliveaux. The police jury is considering whether to support the state’s effort to land a “Nuclear Lifecycle Innovation Campus,” a designation that federal officials say could attract up to $50 billion in private-sector investment.

Neighboring West Feliciana is home to one of the state’s two nuclear power plants, River Bend near St. Francisville.

West Feliciana Parish President Kenny Havard said he has taken part in the talks and has also spoken to officials at Curio Energy, a startup company pitching a fuel-rod recycling plant. Courreges said officials with Curio have participated in some of the state meetings with local officials.

Curio wants to build a plant to recycle spent rods now being stored at nuclear plants across the nation into reusable nuclear fuel or into other material for commercial and medical purposes, according to the company.

In addition to River Bend, West and East Feliciana have ample land and Mississippi River and railroad access to attract nuclear industry companies, officials have pointed out.

Havard said he believes Louisiana may have three or four potential areas for one of the campuses. He stressed the preliminary nature of the discussions in the Felicianas.

"There's been nothing set in stone, no property purchased or bought, you know, any of that stuff, but we are having conversations," he said.

Oliveaux cautioned that he didn't know what talks other East Feliciana officials may have had, noting the concept is still in the early stages and would not move forward without public input first.

Courreges said the state isn’t ruling out locating different nuclear industries in different parts of the state.

Officials with Curio — based in Washington, D.C. — couldn’t be reached for comment.

Company CEO Ed McGinnis spoke to Louisiana lawmakers in a committee hearing last year. McGinnis, a Jefferson Parish native, said material from the recycled rods is an untapped energy source.

McGinnis said the spent rods, which would be held in specialized containment, could be moved to the recycling site by road, rail or water. He pointed out that the federal government's site for permanent storage for nuclear waste, Yucca Mountain in Nevada, hasn't opened nearly three decades after its planned start date.
