title: Why climate action now comes down to speed, finance and cooperation | UN News
authors: UN News, © Climate Visuals, Aji Styawan, Kiara Worth, © Adobe Stock, Fahad Kaizer
description:
Climate action since the Paris Agreement has lowered that trajectory to 2.3°C if current national commitments are fully delivered.
Against that backdrop, the next phase of climate action is less about setting new promises than delivering on those already made, while pushing ambition much further.
Even if current national climate plans and additional net-zero pledges are fully implemented, warming could still peak at around 1.8°C, according to a recent UN Environment Programme report.
Countries responsible for nearly 90 per cent of global emissions have submitted updated national climate plans, known as NDCs.
Cooperation can help countries speed up the renewable energy transition, strengthen resilience and make finance easier to access.
text:
Just over a decade ago, the world was heading towards more than 4°C of warming over pre-industrial levels. Climate action since the Paris Agreement has lowered that trajectory to 2.3°C if current national commitments are fully delivered.

The United Nations has been at the centre of those efforts, pushing for stronger national plans, a faster transition to renewable energy and greater attention to adaptation, climate justice and the financing needs of developing countries.

But progress to limit warming has come as the climate itself continues to heat up. The past 11 years have been the hottest on record, with heat, drought, floods, storms and wildfires taking a growing toll on lives, economies and development.

And the world is still on course to exceed the 1.5°C threshold, at least temporarily.

Against that backdrop, the next phase of climate action is less about setting new promises than delivering on those already made, while pushing ambition much further.

What is a 1.5°C overshoot?

The 1.5°C limit refers to the average rise in global temperature above pre-industrial levels over decades. It is not determined by a single unusually hot year.

An overshoot means temperatures rise above that threshold for a period, reach a peak and, if emissions are cut deeply enough, eventually begin to fall again.

But that decline is not guaranteed, it will depend on the choices governments make now and in the years ahead.

Even if current national climate plans and additional net-zero pledges are fully implemented, warming could still peak at around 1.8°C, according to a recent UN Environment Programme report.

That difference may sound small, but it matters. The higher temperatures climb, and the longer they stay there, the greater the risks.

“Every fraction of a degree will cost lives, destroy livelihoods, deepen inequality, and push ecosystems closer to irreversible damage,” Secretary General António Guterres has warned.

Why does speed matter?

The pace of action matters because the gap between current plans and what the science requires remains very large.

Countries responsible for nearly 90 per cent of global emissions have submitted updated national climate plans, known as NDCs. But even if those plans are fully implement, they are expected to reduce emissions by only around 10 per cent by 2035.

To keep the 1.5°C goal within reach, emissions would need to fall by roughly 60 per cent over the same period.

Closing that gap means faster cuts in emissions, particularly methane and other short lived climate pollutants, while halting deforestation and accelerating the shift from fossil fuels to renewable energy.

Countries also need the infrastructure to support that shift, including modern electricity grids, more storage and greater use of clean electricity in transport, heating and industry.

Moving faster can also strengthen energy security. Three out of four people live in countries that import more fossil fuels than they export, leaving them vulnerable when conflict or other disruptions affect global supplies and prices. Renewable energy can reduce that dependence.

As Guterres has put it, “there are no embargoes on sunshine and no price spikes for wind.”

Why is finance so important?

Not all countries have the same resources to make the shift to clean energy.

Developing countries often face much higher borrowing costs for renewable energy projects, making investment in clean power, grids and storage harder even where the potential is enormous.

The UN has repeatedly called for cheaper finance, reforms to multilateral development banks and greater private investment in developing countries.

Finance also shapes who benefits from the transition. A just transition should help workers and communities adapt to economic change, create decent jobs and give developing countries a larger role in the growing clean-energy economy.

That includes the minerals needed for batteries and other technologies: Producing countries should be able to capture more value from those resources rather than simply exporting raw materials.

Why does adaptation matter ?

Cutting emissions is essential to limit future warming, but it cannot erase the climate impacts that people are already experiencing today.

The recent floods and landslides in Nepal and China have again shown how exposed communities and infrastructure are to extreme weather. A strong El Niño expected to persist into early 2027 could add to those risks in several regions, including the Greater Horn of Africa and parts of Latin America and the Caribbean.

This is why adaptation is so important. In practice, it means helping people and countries cope with the effects of climate change that can no longer be avoided.

In practice, this can include building stronger roads, homes and public services; supporting more resilient agriculture and ecosystems; improving water management; and expanding early-warning systems so communities have more time to prepare for floods, droughts, storms and heatwaves.

Adaptation also needs more funding, especially for the countries and communities most vulnerable to climate impacts and already dealing with climate-related loss and damage

Why do we need cooperation?

No country can tackle climate change entirely on its own.

Governments set their own climate policies, but many of the systems needed to make them work cross borders, from energy markets and finance to technology and supply chains. Greenhouse gas emissions do not stop at national borders either.

Cooperation can help countries speed up the renewable energy transition, strengthen resilience and make finance easier to access.

That does not mean everyone has to move at the same pace. Some have more resources and capacity, while others face much higher financial or technological barriers.

The challenge is to help more countries overcome those barriers and move faster, even as geopolitical tensions currently make international cooperation harder.

Road to the General Assembly

Those priorities are at the centre of the Secretary General’s Climate Summit on 23 September at UN Headquarters. Its objectives can be summed up in three phrases: accelerate the transition, unlock finance and protect people.

The meeting will bring together governments, development banks, business, finance and civil society to focus on practical barriers to implementation.

Also, as part of the Summit, Solutions Dialogues will take place during the week, focusing on practical ways to accelerate action on energy, oceans, adaptation, methane, finance, information integrity and green industrialization.

The focus is on turning existing commitments into action and on what can be done together to accelerate delivery.

You can follow the summit on UNWebTV.

title: Trump administration issues new orders to keep Indiana coal plants open
description:
The Trump administration on Friday issued new orders to continue operations at two Indiana coal plants that had previously been set for retirement.
Schahfer Generating Station in northwest Indiana and F.B.
Culley Generating Station in southwest Indiana must remain running through mid-December.
The Schahfer Generating Station is operated by Merrillville-based Northern Indiana Public Service Co., or NIPSCO, while the Culley Generating Station is operated by Houston-based CenterPoint Energy.
Both companies have previously indicated plans to recover costs for keeping the plants open through the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission, or FERC.
text:
The Trump administration on Friday issued new orders to continue operations at two Indiana coal plants that had previously been set for retirement.

The orders signed by U.S. Secretary of Energy Chris Wright said the coal-fired units at the R.M. Schahfer Generating Station in northwest Indiana and F.B. Culley Generating Station in southwest Indiana must remain running through mid-December.

The Schahfer Generating Station is operated by Merrillville-based Northern Indiana Public Service Co., or NIPSCO, while the Culley Generating Station is operated by Houston-based CenterPoint Energy.

Both utility companies had planned to retire the coal-fired units at their respective stations at the end of 2025. However, the Trump administration ordered the utilities to keep them open for an additional 90 days. Those orders were extended in March and again in June.

In a news release Saturday, the U.S. Department of Energy said having the coal-fired units open has proven critical “during periods of high energy demand and low levels of intermittent energy production.”

“Forcing reliable, dispatchable coal generation off the grid would compromise energy reliability and needlessly raises energy costs for Americans,” Wright said in written remarks. “Midwestern families should not be forced to pay the price for the misguided energy subtraction policies of the past. They deserve affordable, reliable, and secure energy, regardless of the wind blowing or the sun shining.”

The new orders will go be in effect from Sept. 20 through Dec. 18.

The Energy Department said keeping the two Indiana plants open will help maintain reliability for the Midcontinent Independent System Operator, or MISO, which manages the grid across much of the Midwest

In a statement to Inside INdiana Business, NIPSCO said it continues to comply with the Energy Department’s orders regarding the Schahfer Generation Station and assess the impact of the orders on the company’s operations, employees and customers.

“Units 17 and 18 are currently offline while inspections, maintenance and repair work continue, including significant turbine and boiler work,” the company said. “Following the orders, these units will continue to support reliability across the Midcontinent Independent System Operator’s (MISO) Northern and Central Zones.”

CenterPoint also said it would comply with the new orders.

“At this time, there are no direct bill impacts to CenterPoint customers, but we remain committed to keeping customer affordability top-of-mind as we plan for recovery of costs associated with operating the unit,” the company said in a statement to IIB. “We will continue to work collaboratively with federal, state and local stakeholders and remain focused on delivering reliable electric service to our southwestern Indiana customers and their families.”

The new orders came just one week after a panel of federal judges ruled a similar order for Michigan-based Consumers Energy Co. planned to keep its coal-fired J.H Campbell Generating Plant open was illegal.

Public disclosures from NIPSCO and CenterPoint have indicated that their respective coal units are losing money.

Both companies have previously indicated plans to recover costs for keeping the plants open through the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission, or FERC. NIPSCO said FERC has “authorized MISO to adopt a tariff to permit NIPSCO to seek recovery of costs” to comply with the order.

The utilities also indicated they would file rate cases with the Indiana Utility Regulatory Commission. However, IBJ reported that the utilities separately indicated that they only plan to seek rate recovery at the state-level if full costs are not recovered through FERC.

This story has been updated with comments from NIPSCO and CenterPoint. IBJ’s Joey Harris contributed to this story.

The Midwest Ozone Group (“MOG”) submitted August 21st comments to the United States Environmental Protection Agency (“EPA”) addressing the proposed rule that the federal agency describes as streamlining:

… the New Source Review (“NSR”) permitting process for minor sources by eliminating the minimum federal regulatory requirements for public participation.

See 91 Fed. Reg. 41,591 (July 7, 2026).

EPA stated that the proposed rule will make decisions about public participation requirements for State and local minor NSR programs be turned over to the respective State and local air agencies. The stated purpose is to align its regulations with what it characterizes as the “best reading of the Clean Air Act.”

MOG is an affiliation of companies and associations that is stated to draw upon its collective resources to seek solutions to the development of legally and technically sound air quality programs that may impact their facilities, their employees, their communities, their contractors, and the consumers of their products.

MOG's primary efforts are characterized as working with policy makers in evaluating air quality policies by encouraging the use of sound science.

The list of the members of the Midwest Ozone Group include:

Ameren

American Electric Power

American Forest & Paper Association

American Iron and Steel Institute

American Wood Council

Appalachian Region Independent Power Producers Association

Associated Electric Cooperative

Berkshire Hathaway Energy

Big Rivers Electric Corp.

Citizens Energy Group

City Water, Light & Power (Springfield IL)

Cleveland Cliffs Inc.

Council of Industrial Boiler Owners, East Kentucky Power Cooperative

ExxonMobil

Hoosier Energy REC, Inc.

Indiana Energy Association

Indiana-Kentucky Electric Corporation

Indiana Municipal Power Agency

LGE/ KU

Marathon Petroleum Company

Monongahela Power Company

National Lime Association

North American Stainless

Nucor Corporation

Ohio Utility Group

Ohio Valley Electric Corporation

Olympus Power

Steel Manufacturers Association

Wabash Valley Power Alliance

The MOG comments characterize EPA as recognizing:

… inconsistencies between historical programs established by states prior to June 18, 1973, when EPA promulgated the requirements now found at 40 CFR 51.161 that require a “30-day period for submittal of public comment’’ (citing 91 Fed. Reg. 41596).

They also characterize EPA’s position in the proposal as indicating that the participation process for states and local agencies is that it “does not believe that minor source public participation is generally ‘necessary to assure that [the NAAQS] are achieved’ in the context of developing a program for the ‘regulation of’ minor source construction and modification,” (91 Fed. Reg. 41597) adding that “the approach proposed in this action would enable air agencies to retain or establish public participation requirements for review of regulated minor source construction and minor modifications when they believe public participation is desirable, consistent with the Clean Air Act and Federal regulations.”

MOG also states that “[i]n reviewing SIP submissions, the EPA would not expect, whether informally on a case-by-case basis or formally as a minimum requirement set out in regulation, that States include minor NSR public participation for the SIP to be approved as containing sufficient regulatory provisions ‘as necessary to assure that [the NAAQS] are achieved.

The EPA proposal is described as providing states the flexibility to include appropriate public participation elements at their discretion and to tailor those elements to particular circumstances, so long as they are consistent with the Clean Air Act and applicable Federal regulations. MOG agrees with this approach.

The MOG comments address four of the five areas that EPA seeks input for, responding:

Believes that the revisions proposed, if finalized, would reduce the burdens on State and local air agencies that exist under the current regulatory scheme.

Believes that the proposed revisions are the most effective alternative to the current regulatory scheme that fails to recognize the significant differences between the air impacts of major and minor sources with respect to the acquisition of feedback through the public participation process.

Believes that the proposed action adequately addresses relevant reliance interests.

Believes that State and local air agencies that do not find that a revision to minor NSR program’s public participation requirements is administrative or procedural in nature this list of characteristics can provide a sufficient description of the analysis of characteristics considered in adopting the revision to minor NSR program public participation requirements such that EPA will be able to determine whether it agrees with that determination and whether to approve or return the revision to the State or local agency for amendments in accordance with the EPA decision.

text:
On Wednesday, September 16th, 2026, G20 Energy Ministers concluded the Energy Abundance Ministerial in Houston, Texas. The Ministerial was hosted by the White House National Energy Dominance Council (NEDC), the Department of the Interior, the Department of Energy, and the Environmental Protection Agency.

At the conclusion of the Ministerial, G20 Ministers reached consensus on four outcomes advancing energy access, infrastructure development, water resilience, and supply chain security. The outcomes advance the Energy Abundance Working Group’s three pillars: Energy Security and Affordable Baseload, Permitting and Regulatory Efficiency, and Critical Minerals and Resilient Supply Chains. Together, they support the common sense solutions that President Trump has championed to increase energy availability, speed the development of critical infrastructure, strengthen water resilience, and reduce vulnerabilities in the supply chains essential to modern economies.

Ministers reached consensus on deliverables that support affordable, scalable, and context-specific pathways to expand household energy access, including the use of liquefied petroleum gas, or LPG, where it is a reliable and scalable means of rapidly displacing traditional biomass. They also reached agreement on Permitting and Regulatory Efficiency to encourage more efficient, predictable, and effective domestic permitting and regulatory processes, and a Water Reuse Initiative outlining voluntary, fit-for-purpose water reuse to strengthen resilience for communities, energy production, manufacturing, agriculture, and other critical sectors. Finally, Ministers agreed in the Critical Minerals Statement on voluntary cooperation to build resilient, affordable, secure, and diversified critical minerals value chains through information sharing, innovation, investment, capacity building, and local value addition.

“The world cannot build secure energy systems, advanced manufacturing capacity, or digital infrastructure on fragile mineral supply chains,” said Secretary of the Interior Doug Burgum, Chair of the National Energy Dominance Council. “The consensus reached in Houston supports a common sense approach: diversify supply, strengthen domestic and regional capacity, encourage investment and innovation, and respect each nation’s sovereignty over its natural resources. These steps will help reduce overreliance on any single supplier while creating more durable supply chains and greater economic opportunity.”

“Energy is the essential ingredient that enables everything we do,” said Secretary of Energy Chris Wright. “A highly energized society brings health, wealth, and opportunity. The consensus reached in Houston advances cooperation to expand the affordable, reliable, and secure energy, infrastructure, and supply chains needed to support prosperity, resilience, and opportunity throughout the world.”

“President Trump’s energy abundance agenda reflects reality – strong environmental stewardship and economic prosperity go hand in hand,” said Environmental Protection Agency Administrator Lee Zeldin. “The consensus reached in Houston advances solutions that streamline processes without sacrificing safeguards, expand water resilience, and enable the infrastructure needed to deliver reliable and affordable energy. This is how the G20 can support growth, protect communities, and meet the demands of the future.”

The investments and agreements announced in Houston demonstrate how President Trump’s energy abundance agenda is creating jobs, delivering economic opportunity, strengthening American manufacturing, and expanding the energy infrastructure needed to power the future. The Japanese company Hitachi Energy announced a $528 million investment to build a new power transformer manufacturing facility in Gallman, Mississippi, expected to create 654 new jobs. Houston-based Caturus announced a five-train expansion of its Commonwealth LNG export facility in Louisiana that would add 7.75 million tonnes per annum of capacity and nearly double the project’s planned capacity to approximately 17.25 million tonnes per annum, Continental Resources signed a memorandum of understanding with Venezuela’s PDVSA to develop and operate the 126,000-acre Ayacucho 2 Block in the Orinoco Belt, which Continental estimates contains approximately 30 billion barrels of oil.

At the Ministerial, Administrator Zeldin announced the EPA’s repeal of the majority of the Biden Administration’s greenhouse gas requirements for U.S. power plants, the largest power sector deregulatory action in American history. EPA projects the repeal will save $310 billion and help unleash America’s vast energy resources, including coal and natural gas. The Administrator also proposed to repeal the remaining power sector standards, which would save an additional $370 million in direct compliance costs. Together, these actions will restore reliable, affordable baseload power and strengthen American energy dominance.

Representatives from the following nations and unions were present at the three-day Ministerial: the African Union, the Argentine Republic, the Commonwealth of Australia, the Federative Republic of Brazil, Canada, the People’s Republic of China, the European Union, the French Republic, the Federal Republic of Germany, the Republic of India, the Republic of Indonesia, the Italian Republic, Japan, the United Mexican States, the Republic of Poland, the Russian Federation, the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia, the Republic of Korea, the Republic of Türkiye, and the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland.

Instituted by the Biden administration, the Solar For All program planned to assist up to 900,000 low-income American households with residential solar.

text:
By Martin McConnell

A lawsuit pitting the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) against the Rhode Island American Federation of Labor and Congress of Industrial Organizations (AFL-CIO) labor union and other plaintiffs has reached its conclusion, with potentially massive implications for the American solar industry.

Judge Mary S. McElroy of the U.S. District Court for the District of Rhode Island has ruled in favor of the union. Specifically, McElroy and the court state that the EPA’s 2025 termination of the Biden-era Solar For All (SFA) program is unlawful thanks to rescinding of already-allocated federal funds. In turn, the court has ordered the federal agency to reinstate the renewable energy program.

In her decision, McElroy writes that the second Trump administration’s One Big Beautiful Bill Act, passed in summer 2025, “did not convert the obligated SFA grants into lumpsum appropriations that EPA had unilateral discretion to administer.” Because the EPA’s rescinding of funds included grants that were already awarded, the court rules that the misappropriation of funds is in violation of a direct order from Congress.

“Instead, Congress’s clear intent was that EPA continue to administer the already obligated SFA grants,” she says. “Defendants acted contrary to this intent, and with no other statutory authority, when they terminated the SFA program. The Termination Decision was therefore contrary to law and in excess of its statutory authority, in violation of the (Administrative Procedure Act).”

Potential impact nationwide

The EPA is currently reviewing the court order and considering an appeal, according to officials. Should that appeal either be struck down or go unheard completely, the impacts of McElroy’s decision could have wide-reaching implications throughout the entire energy sector.

Instituted by the Biden administration, the Solar For All program planned to assist up to 900,000 low-income American households with residential solar. Coupled with major tax incentives for solar energy through the Inflation Reduction Act, the program may have heralded a shift in the American energy market as a whole, had it stayed through the beginning of President Trump’s second term.

“Clean, affordable power like solar shouldn’t be a closed-door luxury,” says Alex St. Pierre, VP for environmental justice at the Conservation Law Foundation (CLF), in a statement by the Southern Environmental Law Center (SELC). “Solar for All was built to open that door, and EPA tried to slam it shut.

“Today’s ruling pushes it back open. Communities have waited long enough. Nearly every family is looking for ways to cut their energy bill. These dollars should go where Congress intended: toward lower energy bills, less climate pollution, good jobs, and cleaner air.”

Jillian Blanchard, SVP of climate change and environmental justice at Lawyers for Good Government (L4GG), says the decision “makes clear that EPA unlawfully terminated the Solar for All Program.” While the ultimate fate of the Solar For All program remains uncertain, law officials across the energy space say its potential full reinstatement is a major blow to the Trump administration’s cost-cutting efforts when it comes to Biden-era energy policies.

“Today’s ruling confirms what we have argued from the beginning: EPA cannot erase a $7 billion program that Congress created and funded,” says Jillian Blanchard, SVP of climate change and environmental justice at Lawyers for Good Government (L4GG). “For more than a year, families and communities have seen higher energy bills while billions of dollars intended to lower electricity costs sat out of reach. Today’s decision makes clear that EPA unlawfully terminated the Solar for All Program.”

text:
BALTIMORE, PLANO, Texas and AUSTIN, Texas (Sept. 21, 2026) — Constellation (Nasdaq: CEG), the nation's largest producer of clean, emissions-free, reliable energy, and Toyota Motor North America today announced a 15-year renewable energy agreement that supports the development of new solar generation and advances Toyota's sustainability goals. With this agreement, Toyota will receive renewable energy certificates (RECs) generated by the Milano Solar project, developed by Ferrovial, a leading global infrastructure company, through the Constellation Offsite Renewable (CORe) solutions product.

Backed by Toyota's long-term commitment, Constellation has entered into a separate long-term power purchase agreement (PPA) with Ferrovial's Milano Solar project for more than 115 megawatts of solar capacity, representing approximately 246,000 megawatt-hours of renewable energy generation annually. The agreement represents a portion of the total output from Milano Solar, a 203.97-megawatt project located in Milam County, Texas.

"Companies are looking for practical ways to meet their sustainability goals while supporting the development of new clean energy resources," said Dan Verbanac, senior vice president, Retail and Solutions, Constellation. "By connecting Toyota with a large-scale renewable project like Milano Solar, Constellation is helping deliver meaningful environmental benefits and bring additional clean energy to the grid."

Toyota will receive project-specific Renewable Energy Certificates (RECs) generated by Milano Solar and retired by Constellation throughout the 15-year term of the agreement. The project is expected to begin commercial operation in September 2027.

"Toyota works to embody our core value of Respect for the Planet through carbon neutrality programs, including power purchase agreements such as this," said Tim Hilgeman, Toyota general manager of environmental sustainability. "With Constellation and Ferrovial, we appreciate the science-based approach to one of the most complex challenges of our time."

As part of Toyota's North American 8th Environmental Action Plan, the company aims to match 100 percent of electricity consumption with renewable energy through a combination of Virtual Power Purchase Agreements, Renewable Energy Credits and onsite solar.

"Milano Solar is a strong example of how large-scale renewable projects create lasting value beyond the power they generate," said María José Esteruelas, Ferrovial Energy CEO. "We're proud to deliver durable, long-term benefits to the communities and workforces that make these projects possible, while supporting growing demand for reliable energy infrastructure."

Ferrovial Energy, a division of Ferrovial, is developing the project.

Through Share the Light, Duke Energy is helping ensure that when those moments come, families have somewhere to turn. We are deeply grateful for this partnership and for Duke Energy's commitment to being there for our neighbors when they need a helping hand."

The $1.6 billion investment is designed to strengthen the state’s liquefied natural gas (LNG) corridor, in turn meeting rising demands from LNG exports, power generators, manufacturers and utilities. “More than $48 billion in LNG projects have been announced in Louisiana since 2024, and investment at that scale creates demand for the infrastructure and businesses needed to support it,” said Louisiana Economic Development Secretary Susan B. Bourgeois. “Black Bayou Energy Hub is a direct result of that momentum and an investment in sustaining it. This project strengthens the natural gas infrastructure that will serve major projects already underway while increasing Louisiana’s capacity to compete for what comes next.” Centered on the Black Bayou salt dome in Cameron Parish, the company’s new natural gas infrastructure will extend into nearby Calcasieu Parish to provide blending, balancing, storage and transportation services to LNG exporters and more. Construction is slated to begin in 2026 with full completion expected in 2028. Meanwhile, Black Bayou Energy Hub’s HQ expansion will support its long-term administrative, engineering and operational duties.

INDIA’S AI INFRASTRUCTURE ADVANTAGE

Tata Consultancy Services subsidiary HyperVault has now acquired the land necessary to pursue a new $7.3 billion AI data center campus in Hyderabad, India. The company is looking to introduce a 1-gigawatt data center in the region, as its 264-acre site will deliver a purpose-built campus for AI companies and hyperscalers. The project is anticipated to become one of India’s most advanced and largest AI infrastructure campuses, supported by its green energy and water-neutral design. “HyperVault advances TCS’ Infrastructure-to-Intelligence strategy by bringing together AI-ready infrastructure with our cloud, engineering, enterprise transformation and AI capabilities,” said Tata Consultancy Services CEO K Krithivasan. “Hyderabad offers the scale, talent and ecosystem to serve global customers.” The project will create thousands of direct and indirect jobs in the region.

THE RIGHT INGREDIENTS TO DRAW IN GIVAUDAN

Switzerland-based flavor, fragrance and cosmetic ingredient manufacturer Givaudan will strengthen its North American portfolio by establishing new operations in Indiana. The company selected the town of West Harrison, located in Dearborn County, for its new $215 million liquids production facility. This investment will support the construction of a 78,000-sq.-ft. plant near the Indiana-Ohio state line, a site that was targeted to help the company meet regional demand. “This new facility represents our continued investment and long-term confidence in our North American operations,” said Givaudan North American President, Taste & Wellbeing Mindy Kucks. “It demonstrates the importance of the market to Givaudan and to the food and beverage industry, while keeping our growth rooted in the Greater Cincinnati regional economy. It will continue to strengthen our market and operational presence and advance the sustainable, innovative solutions that consumers love.” The company currently operates 17 locations in North America and has said it will create over 250 new jobs in Indiana by 2031. Construction of the new facility will begin in 2026 with initial operations anticipated to begin in 2028.

description:

text:
Nearly 1 billion people live in C40 cities. Mayors see firsthand the challenges people face and the solutions that can make a difference.

The Urban 20 (U20) brings together cities to develop shared recommendations that push for action on city priorities and needs in G20 discussions.

Over 30 cities came together for this year’s U20, co-hosted by Los Angeles and New York, to identify shared priorities, asks, and opportunities for action on some of the world’s most pressing challenges.

When a city succeeds, we know there is potential for all cities to succeed.

Mayor of New York City, Zohran Mamdani

Cities are stronger when they work together

The first day of U20 focused on collaboration and highlighted how mayors are working together to address the key priorities of this year’s cycle:

Affordable housing

Climate action

Sustainability

Resilience

Protecting immigrant communities and human mobility

C40 Co-Chair and Mayor of Freetown, Yvonne Aki-Sawyerr, shared the work of C40 mayors, how they are implementing bold climate action and highlighted where greater co-operation can help them go further.

Mayors came to New York from different countries and different circumstances, but the pressures facing our residents are remarkably similar: rising costs, extreme heat, housing insecurity and displacement.

C40 Co-Chair and Mayor of Freetown, Yvonne Aki-Sawyerr

C40’s Executive Director, Mark Watts, spoke about the urgency of the moment and the need for collective action across cities, governments, and civil society, and mayors set out what they need to deliver more for their residents – including stronger partnerships, better policies and greater support from national governments.

For all of us, what binds us, whether Rome or Freetown or Mexico City, we know that oftentimes it is mayors and it is cities that have to deal with the crises of people most directly. And we believe that cities also have many of the answers.

Mayor of New York City, Zohran Mamdani

Cutting costs, creating jobs and strengthening local economies

City leaders also explored how the clean-energy transition can cut costs, create good jobs and bring new investment into communities.

The Mayor of Paris, Emmanuel Grégoire, the Mayor of Amsterdam, Femke Halsema and the Governor of Jakarta, Pramono Anung, shared how their cities are ensuring the benefits of the clean-energy transition reach everyone and what a just urban transition looks like in practice.

Showcasing urban climate action that improves residents’ lives

Hosted by C40, the Mayor of Helsinki, Daniel Sazonov, the Mayor of Miami, Eileen Higgins and the Mayor of The Hague, Jan van Zanen, explored how cities can leverage the clean-energy transition to build stronger economies, lower costs and create good jobs.

The conversation centred on making sure the tangible benefits of climate investment reach the communities facing the greatest economic and environmental inequality.

For us it’s crucial, if we don’t have the people with us, then we will never get the government with us.

Mayor of Miami, Eileen Higgins

If you want the people with you, you need to make them part of the process – not the audience.

Mayor of The Hague, Jan van Zanen

NYC Chief Climate Officer Louise Yeung closed the session by reflecting on what cities can learn from each other as they work toward a fairer, cleaner future: “We are more powerful when we work together. Climate change is borderless and unrelenting. In turn, we must be unrelenting in our response.”

City leadership needs support at every level of government

Cities can move faster when national governments work with them.

UN-Habitat Executive Director Anacláudia Rossbach joined national representatives to respond to the commitments made by mayors and consider how stronger collaboration between cities, national governments and global institutions can help turn local solutions into broader action.

The communiqué sets out action across three priorities:

Climate and energy: Accelerate a clean and just energy transition that lowers costs, creates good jobs and improves health, while giving cities greater access to climate finance and the tools to protect residents from extreme heat, flooding, wildfire and other worsening climate impacts. Mayors call for better access to climate and health data to expand and accelerate the roll-out of early warning systems.

Housing: Expand access to affordable, resilient homes, protect tenants, and tackle homelessness. Mayors call for greater local authority over housing and better access to public and international finance for locally led solutions.

Migration: Support newcomers while maintaining strong public services and social cohesion for all residents. Cities call for a greater role in migration policy and direct funding for reception, integration and essential services.

This communiqué turns that shared experience into a shared agenda for action. Cities are ready to deliver. Give us the tools and resources to act, and we will.

C40 Co-Chair and Mayor of Freetown, Yvonne Aki-Sawyerr

TD financing will help nearly double the Maine sawmill’s lumber production, create and retain 220 quality jobs and strengthen the rural Aroostook County economy.

MOUNT LAUREL, NJ, Sept. 21, 2026 — TD Bank U.S. has partnered with Irving Forest Products, Inc., a subsidiary of J.D. Irving, Limited, in undertaking a modernization project to expand the Ashland Sawmill in Nashville Plantation, Maine. The project will increase production while building on the mill’s history of contributing to the economic resiliency of the Aroostook community.

When complete, the Ashland Sawmill project will double the facility’s annual lumber production capacity from 130 million to 250 million board feet while strengthening its role as a leading manufacturer of dimensional lumber. The project is expected to create and retain the equivalent of 220 permanent, full-time jobs while supporting upstream workers, including foresters and loggers throughout the region. All jobs provide a full benefits package and pay at or above a living wage for Aroostook County.

Key Points

The Ashland Sawmill expansion will nearly double annual lumber production, helping meet demand and strengthen the regional supply of building materials.

The project will create and retain the equivalent of 220 full-time jobs with benefits and living wages, while supporting foresters, loggers and other workers across the region.

Public tax credit programs are helping attract private investment to a rural community where the sawmill is a major employer.

TD Community Development Corporation provided a $10 million New Markets Tax Credit allocation and supported $49 million in investments and bridge financing to move the project forward.

The project is supported by the Federal New Markets Tax Credit (NMTC) program and the Maine New Markets Capital Investment Program, which together bring a combined total of $112.9 million of tax credit allocations to the project to help bridge a funding gap by stimulating private investment. The state portion was previously announced by the Finance Authority of Maine (FAME) in June.

TD Community Development Corporation provided $10 million in a New Markets Tax Credit allocation and supported $49 million in NMTC investments, including federal and state investments and bridge equity, to help advance the Ashland Sawmill modernization project.

“The Ashland Sawmill expansion shows how New Markets Tax Credits can bring private investment to rural communities and support businesses critical to local and regional economies,” said Will Richter, TD CDC Senior Relationship Manager, TD Bank U.S. “Lumber production has long been an important part of Maine’s economic infrastructure and the broader New England supply chain, and the modernization of the Ashland Sawmill will help Irving Forest Products continue creating jobs, supporting families and strengthening the communities it serves.”

The NMTC and Maine New Markets Capital Investment programs catalyze private investment in low-income communities through tax credits, enabling economic development. They are administered by Community Development Financial Institutions Fund (CDFI Fund) and FAME, respectively.

“We deeply appreciate the support of the CDFI Fund, FAME and the CDEs for this important project,” said Jerome Pelletier of Irving Forest Products, Inc. “We are also grateful to Senator Susan Collins for her longstanding support of Maine’s forest products sector. This investment reflects the hard work of our team and our long-term commitment to the region. It will help us support good jobs and continue contributing to the Aroostook community.”

We are grateful for Senator Susan Collins, whose continued support for economic growth and modern rail service in Maine has helped create opportunities for investments like this one.”

title: IRENA Examines How Auction Design Can Strengthen Renewable Energy Supply Chain Resilience
description:
Key Details The International Renewable Energy Agency’s Addressing Renewable Energy Supply Chain Risks report links supply-chain resilience directly to the design of renewable energy auctions and the industrial policies supporting them.
Manufacturing Resilience Requires More Than Procurement Rules Local-content rules can create demand but cannot by themselves build competitive manufacturing.
IRENA links auction design with industrial strategy, trade, R&D, finance, mineral processing, skills and recycling.
Countries can combine selective domestic manufacturing with supplier diversification, regional production, multiple trade routes, recycling and strategic reserves.
Policy Relevance For India, the challenge is to pursue rapid renewable deployment and deeper domestic manufacturing without making one undermine the other.
text:
Key Details

The International Renewable Energy Agency’s Addressing Renewable Energy Supply Chain Risks report links supply-chain resilience directly to the design of renewable energy auctions and the industrial policies supporting them.

India’s position illustrates both the progress and the remaining concentration:

India received only 1% of global investment in energy-transition manufacturing facilities during 2018–2024, compared with more than 80% for China.

India produced an estimated 4.5% of the world’s solar modules in 2024. Installed module-manufacturing capacity reached 68.2 GW, but production was about 34.2 GW, reflecting capacity utilisation of roughly 50%.

Indian wind-turbine manufacturers secured around 0.8% of global turbine orders in 2024.

Low Tariffs Can Leave Projects Exposed

Renewable auctions have lowered electricity prices through competitive long-term contracts, but low fixed bids can become difficult to deliver when equipment and financing costs rise before commissioning.

Between 2020 and 2022, higher polysilicon, metal and freight costs increased estimated investment costs for new utility-scale solar and wind projects by 15–25% globally. In India, the lowest solar tariff rose from ₹1.99/kWh in December 2020 to ₹2.35/kWh in February 2022 as imported input costs increased.

IRENA therefore argues that auction performance should be assessed not only by the winning tariff, but also by project realisation, delivery time and system cost.

Indexation Can Allocate Cost Risk in Advance

Contract indexation links project remuneration to agreed benchmarks such as inflation, commodity prices, interest rates or exchange rates. It can cover the entire tariff or only cost components particularly exposed to external shocks.

This allows developers to retain ordinary commercial risk while specified exceptional cost movements are shared with procurers or consumers. The trade-off is between greater project-delivery certainty and potentially higher tariffs or public costs.

Other mechanisms can reduce risk in different ways: longer lead times, graduated bonds and penalties, and pre-arranged land, permits and grid access. Contract reopening can rescue projects after exceptional shocks, but routine renegotiation can undermine auction credibility.

India’s solar-park model and partial grid reservation are cited as examples of reducing post-auction development uncertainty.

India’s ALMM Experience Shows the Localisation Trade-Off

IRENA uses India’s Approved List of Models and Manufacturers (ALMM) to examine how domestic-content requirements interact with renewable deployment.

During the 2022–23 implementation episode, no foreign manufacturers had been admitted to the list and approved annual module capacity stood at 21.7 GW by January 2023. Supply constraints and project delays contributed to a temporary suspension of the requirement.

This is historical rather than the current position. ALMM is now operational and has expanded to include a separate solar-cell list, first issued in July 2025 and subsequently updated.

Earlier Indian auction evidence shows the trade-off more clearly: the local-content segment attracted bids for around 700 MW, compared with 1,470 MW in the unrestricted segment, while one study estimated electricity costs about 6% higher. Completion rates were nevertheless broadly comparable, and evidence on longer-term manufacturing and innovation gains was mixed.

The issue is therefore not localisation itself, but whether its timing and scope match domestic productive capacity, technological competitiveness and the deployment pipeline.

Manufacturing Resilience Requires More Than Procurement Rules

Local-content rules can create demand but cannot by themselves build competitive manufacturing. IRENA links auction design with industrial strategy, trade, R&D, finance, mineral processing, skills and recycling.

Successful localisation generally requires a large and predictable project pipeline that gives manufacturers confidence to invest. In smaller or less mature markets, rigid requirements can instead reduce competition without creating an efficient domestic industry.

Resilience also need not mean producing every component domestically. Countries can combine selective domestic manufacturing with supplier diversification, regional production, multiple trade routes, recycling and strategic reserves.

Policy Relevance

For India, the challenge is to pursue rapid renewable deployment and deeper domestic manufacturing without making one undermine the other.

Allocate auction risks upfront: Contracts can specify which risks remain with developers and which exceptional movements qualify for indexation, reducing reliance on later renegotiation.

Measure localisation by outcomes, not factory capacity alone: Capacity utilisation, upstream dependence, bidder participation, tariffs and project commissioning can show whether ALMM requirements are strengthening resilience without constraining deployment.

Move deeper into the value chain: The industrial opportunity extends beyond module assembly to cells, wafers, inverters, equipment, storage components, critical minerals and recycling.

Coordinate procurement with industrial policy: Alignment among MNRE, the Ministry of Power, SECI and industrial-policy institutions will determine whether renewable demand translates into competitive domestic capability.

name: Louisiana Environment
title: Liberty vs. the Leviathan: Banning Diesel Exports Won't Lower Your Fuel Bill — It'll Raise It
description:
Diesel prices have gotten out of hand.
You read that right: a policy sold as lowering diesel prices would tighten the gasoline market too, hitting every driver in the state, not just truckers.
Once government gets a taste of picking winners and losers in energy markets, it rarely gives that power back.
Finalizing that rule with the current small refinery exemptions preserved or, better yet, repealing it altogether, would do more to ease prices than a new export ban ever could.
The honest fix for high diesel prices isn’t a ban, it’s more supply.
text:
Diesel prices have gotten out of hand. Every trucker, farmer, and small business owner in Louisiana feels it every time they fill up. So when Washington starts talking about “fixing” it, it’s worth paying close attention. Unfortunately, the fix on the table right now would make things worse, not better.

Here’s the idea making the rounds in the Capitol: ban U.S. companies from exporting diesel. Senate Majority Leader John Thune said this week he’s willing to consider the idea, reasoning that if we’re producing diesel and shipping it overseas while Americans pay record prices at home, keeping that fuel here should bring prices down. It sounds simple. It sounds like common sense. It is neither.

It’s important to note that refiners don’t make diesel in isolation. Rather, they make it alongside gasoline.Every barrel of crude that goes into a refinery comes out as a mix of fuels, diesel included. Take away the export market and refiners can’t just keep making the same amount of diesel and stockpile the rest. They have to cut how much crude they run, period. The American Fuel & Petrochemical Manufacturers (AFPM) trade association estimates that could mean up to 4 million fewer barrels of crude processed per day, which would drag gasoline output down with it by something like 2 million barrels a day. You read that right: a policy sold as lowering diesel prices would tighten the gasoline market too, hitting every driver in the state, not just truckers.

This is price-control logic wearing an “energy security” costume, and we’ve seen this movie before.Whether it’s rent control, wage caps, or the credit card interest rate cap Washington flirted with earlier this year, government intervention in prices always produces the same result: less supply, not more, because you can’t repeal the law of supply and demand by executive order. Diesel would be no exception.

Louisiana would take a direct hit.As AFPM’s refiners have laid out, most U.S. refining capacity, and most of the diesel we export, sits right here on the Gulf Coast. The East Coast and West Coast rely on imports because there isn’t enough pipeline or shipping capacity to move fuel from us to them cheaply, so a ban wouldn’t even reroute much Gulf Coast diesel to those markets. What it would do is shrink the market for the fuel Louisiana refiners make, threaten Louisiana refining jobs, and leave import-dependent regions of the country more exposed to a shaky global diesel market, not less.

There’s also a bureaucratic problem lurking underneath all of this. An export ban would hand Washington the power to decide, barrel by barrel, who gets to sell fuel and to whom — a licensing regime run by unelected officials deciding which companies win and which lose, dressed up as a consumer protection. That’s not how free markets work, and it’s exactly the kind of quiet expansion of federal control that starts as an “emergency measure” and never quite goes away. Once government gets a taste of picking winners and losers in energy markets, it rarely gives that power back.

Foreign refiners, meanwhile, would be thrilled.They’d keep buying cheap American crude and exporting the diesel it makes into markets we walked away from — Mexico, Latin America, Europe — while hostile competitors like Russia expand their footprint in those same markets. We’d be handing away energy influence we spent decades building, all while doing nothing to fix the actual cause of high prices: a global supply crunch tied to the wars in Ukraine and the Middle East.

Washington could also help without banning anything at all. EPA is sitting on an overdue Renewable Fuel Standard rule for 2026 and 2027, and the uncertainty around it, including whether small refinery exemptions will be granted or clawed back, is adding its own cost and volatility to diesel markets. Finalizing that rule with the current small refinery exemptions preserved or, better yet, repealing it altogether, would do more to ease prices than a new export ban ever could.

The honest fix for high diesel prices isn’t a ban, it’s more supply. That means permitting reform, pipeline capacity, and policies that let American refiners run flat-out instead of policies that force them to throttle back. At the Pelican Institute, we’ve made that case again and again on energy: Louisiana’s road to lower costs and real energy dominance runs through unleashing production, not restricting it.

text:
Democratic nominee Cait Conley will face incumbent Republican Mike Lawler in NY-17, one of the nation’s most closely watched House races. Here’s where the candidates stand on the environmental issues defining the district.

By Leana Carbonez for Inside Climate News

The Hudson River bisects New York’s 17th Congressional District, with basalt bluffs lining its western bank 40 miles north of New York City.

The district, which includes Putnam and Rockland counties, as well as parts of Dutchess and Westchester, boasts acres of protected parkland. Its lakes and reservoirs feed the Croton Watershed, a significant source of New York City’s drinking water.

This fall, the 17th district is among the most closely watched House races in what many consider the most consequential midterm elections in American history. The Cook Political Report has the district as one of 18 House “Toss-Up” races, and rates it as one of only two with a Democratic lean. This makes it one of the Democrats’ best pickup opportunities, with Republicans holding a slim 218–213 majority in the House.

The race pits Republican incumbent Mike Lawler against Democrat Cait Conley, a veteran and national security expert. She won 49.5 percent of the vote in the June 23 primary, beating Rockland state legislator Beth Davidson, who took 31.8 percent.

With President Donald Trump’s net approval rating at minus-30 among New York voters, according to polling by The Economist, Democrats hope to win over moderate Republicans.

“I am willing to cross party lines and vote for Cait Conley,” said William Knox, a resident of Dutchess County who supported Lawler in both 2022 and 2024. “He has consistently voted along lines that support the president’s agenda, rather than voting in ways that would support us, his constituents.”

Should Democrats win both the House and Senate, the midterms could put Trump’s political future in jeopardy and determine whether the United States returns to the emissions-reduction path set by the Biden administration. As it stands, Climate Action Tracker rates U.S. climate action as “Critically Insufficient.”

As the campaign has worn on, both candidates have sought to cast the other in a partisan light: Conley has painted Lawler as a lapdog of Trump’s “Make America Great Again” agenda, while Lawler has labeled Conley a Democrat allied with New York’s “radical, far-left socialists.” The race has become a mudslinging contest, rife with half-truths, over the Hudson Valley’s pocketbook issues.

Conley has focused her campaign on affordability issues, tying higher gasoline and grocery prices to Lawler’s support for Trump’s war with Iran. Lawler, meanwhile, has blamed Albany Democrats and Gov. Kathy Hochul for soaring utility costs driven by the closure of Indian Point Energy Center, the district’s retired nuclear power plant, and New York’s climate law.

Related | Is this vulnerable New York Republican trying to lose his House seat?

Data centers are another flashpoint. Rockland, where Lawler lives, has five. Lawler has seized on growing public unease over AI, spotlighting more than $328,000 in payments from two AI surveillance companies disclosed in Conley’s financial filings. He has turned a remark made in April, isolated from its context and since clarified by Conley, into a campaign cudgel; her comment, “we need data centers,” anchors a new campaign ad. Conley, in turn, has pointed to Lawler’s record, accusing him of helping turn Rockland into a data-center hub, highlighting campaign donations from Big Tech.

The campaigns have devoted considerable energy to undercutting each other’s claims, while poring over one another’s records.

Lawler won his second term in 2024, picking up 52.1 percent of the vote. He was one of only three Republicans to win a congressional district that Democrat Kamala Harris won in her unsuccessful run for the presidency.

Democrats will be buoyed in the tight race by a sizable voter registration advantage in the district. As of February 2026, there were 194,295 registered Democrats and 138,421 Republicans, widening the gap since the 2024 election.

Many environmentalists across the district are looking for change.

“I’m concerned with the direction in which things are going. And I’m not looking for perfection,” said Kate Schlott, who serves on the Ossining Environmental Advisory Council.

Many of NY-17’s environmental assets are already blighted or under threat:

In the village of Buchanan, in Westchester County, Indian Point is undergoing a $2.3 billion decommissioning project. During its more than 50 years of operation, the plant routinely discharged low levels of treated radioactive wastewater into the Hudson River. But plans to release roughly 45,000 gallons of radioactive wastewater during decommissioning, approved by a court but now under appeal, along with calls to reopen the plant, have made Indian Point a hot political issue ahead of the November elections.

PFAS, man-made “forever chemicals,” contaminate Rockland County’s drinking water, with the Trump administration moving to roll back limits on some PFAS.

A data center in Orangetown, in Rockland County, has plans for a tax-subsidised expansion. The town has passed its own data center moratorium, but it does not apply to the project, and concerns surrounding noise pollution, diesel backup generators and the potential for contaminating the adjacent Lake Tappan Reservoir have mobilized local residents.

In early 2025, Politico reported that $26 million in Biden-era clean energy and climate funding was cut from the district by the Trump administration, including a $19.7 million IBM project set to characterize, track and mitigate methane emissions.

Throughout Conley’s campaign, she has argued that the climate crisis is a national security threat, not simply an environmental issue, a position couched in her experience as director for counterterrorism on the National Security Council during the Biden administration.

Conley opposes cuts to federal residential solar tax credits, supports reinstating clean energy grant programs and has called for modernizing the electric grid. She has also advocated moving away from fossil fuels in favor of solar, geothermal and wind power, while calling for greater accountability from utility companies, promising to haul them into public hearings and subpoena their records.

Conley does not oppose data centers outright.

“My policy on data centers has been very clear. If they’re going to be built, they need to be a net positive for the communities, not extorting the communities that they’re being built in,” she said in an early September interview on CNN’s “State of the Union.”

Lawler, who appeared on the same CNN program, emphasized the importance of preserving local authority over data-center development. Asked about his vote for the House version of the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, which would have barred state and local governments from regulating AI systems, he pointed to the provision’s removal from the final bill and his record of preserving local zoning authority.

He argued that New York’s decision to shut down nuclear plants, ban natural-gas extraction and block pipeline construction is part of the reason New York is struggling to deal with the issue of data centers.

“It’s my opponent, Cait Conley, who is bought and paid for by AI and Big Tech,” he said.

Conley opposes reopening Indian Point, unlike Lawler, who recently brought Energy Secretary Chris Wright to the site. She argues that the plant’s closure reflected the safety standards and technological limitations of its era.

She has not taken a broadly anti-nuclear position. Her stance may reflect a shift in public opinion: about 60 percent of Americans now favor building nuclear power plants, up from 43 percent in 2020, according to a 2025 Pew Research Center survey. And companies like Meta, Microsoft and Amazon are turning to nuclear energy to power their data centers.

After two terms in Congress, Lawler has a more concrete environmental record for voters to consider.

The League of Conservation Voters, which tracks members of Congress’ voting records on environmental legislation, gave Lawler a 12 percent score for 2025. He voted in favor of the environment just four of 33 times, the group found. This marks a decline from his score of 18 percent in 2024 and 19 percent in 2023.

Still, among New York’s seven House Republicans, Lawler, former executive director of the New York State Republican Party, was tied with U.S. Rep. Nick LaLota for the highest 2025 score. He also ranked among the highest-scoring House Republicans nationally. He has supported clean air and water legislation, co-sponsoring the NJ-NY Watershed Protection Act in 2023, which would have established an annual $20 million fund to keep the Hudson River clean, and supporting New York’s Environmental Bond Act, which makes $4.2 billion available for environmental and community projects.

He has also secured $35.9 million in funding for 17 projects across the district, the majority supporting environmental infrastructure, including clean-water and wastewater projects, PFAS treatment, stormwater management and dam rehabilitation aimed at reducing the risk of pollution and flooding.

Lawler has been less supportive of green energy investments, arguing that New York’s climate policies place an undue burden on taxpayers. He was among a group of House Republicans who urged leaders to preserve clean-energy tax credits, warning that eliminating them could jeopardize investments and projects in their districts, but ultimately voted for the One Big Beautiful Bill Act that rolled back many of those subsidies. He has called for the repeal of the state’s landmark Climate Leadership and Community Protection Act.

In op-eds, he pits “basic economics and science” or “commonsense” against “fad green energy policies” advanced by what he calls “far-left” ideologues.

“I am somehow anti-environment for wanting to expand natural gas and nuclear—nonsense,” Lawler wrote.

Lawler co-chairs the House’s Extreme Heat Caucus and the Appalachian National Scenic Trail Caucus, and belongs to the Climate Solutions Caucus, PFAS Task Force and Conservative Climate Caucus. The latter advocates for an energy strategy that emphasises the continued use of fossil fuels—which are damaging the climate, with disastrous effects for New York and the rest of the world—alongside emerging technologies.

Related | Climate ‘overshoot’ is coming—are we ready?

Before entering Congress, Lawler was a registered lobbyist and executive director of New Yorkers for Affordable Energy, a natural-gas advocacy group whose backers included utilities and fossil-fuel interests. And, in this election cycle, Lawler has received campaign donations from a range of oil and gas interests, including $10,000 from Koch Inc.; $5,000 from California-based utility company Edison International; $4,500 from Williams Cos.; and $1,000 from Entergy, the former owner of Indian Point. He has also received personal contributions from industry executives and owners, including $8,300 from the owner of Sunshine Gasoline, a Florida-based oil retailer; $7,000 from the chairman of United Refining Co., based in Warren, Pennsylvania; and $9,500 from the president of Texas Crude Energy.

Conley is part of Unrig Washington, a program in which candidates reject corporate PAC money. While Conley’s campaign website lays out her approach to “Fighting Climate Change as a National Security Priority,” she has not made the issue a major focus of her campaign.

Neither the Conley nor Lawler campaign responded to requests for comment.

Conley and Lawler will face off in a televised debate on Sept. 28 at 8 p.m. Eastern on News 12, followed by another on Oct. 14 at 7 p.m. on PIX11. As the general election draws closer, many are hoping the debates will force the candidates to take clearer, more specific positions on the environmental issues facing the district.

text:
The following is a transcript of a speech delivered by UN Climate Change Executive Secretary Simon Stiell at the Build Clean Now Industry Acceleration Summit on Monday 21 September 2026 in New York City.

Good morning.

It’s a pleasure to join you today.

And I thank the ITA for hosting us.

The new King of New York – Knicks basketball star, Jalen Brunson said: "You’re allowed to think about the worst possible scenario. But you’ve got to go out there and do something about it."

He’s right.

Holding the rise in global temperature to 1.5 degrees Celsius this century is demanded by science, agreed by nations, and essential to protect every person and economy.

Yet exceeding that limit is now guaranteed, at least temporarily. A recent report by the UN Environment Programme reaffirms it.

How to respond?

By doing something about it: Building resilience. And cutting greenhouse gas pollution faster – to bring the temperature rise back below 1.5 degrees as quickly as possible.

That demands international cooperation, laser-focussed on implementation, supporting delivery of the targets, plans and commitments countries have agreed.

Our systems have proven they can drive real change.

UN-convened cooperation – and national efforts – have reduced the projected global temperature rise – from well over 4 degrees Celsius, to 2.6 degrees Celsius – undeniable progress but not enough to avoid catastrophe.

And the Paris Agreement – and other COPs – have helped unleash an energy revolution – even if it’s still globally uneven, and vulnerable countries need support to get fully on board.

Take new data released today by the International Renewable Energy Agency: last year, renewable capacity additions reached a record high: 693GW. That’s over half the installed power capacity of the entire United States.

And thanks to global renewables, humanity avoided almost half a trillion US dollars in fossil fuel costs. Almost half a trillion – that’s a mammoth decarbonisation dividend – that’s more than the national GDP of over three quarters of countries on Earth.

And clean energy’s attracting extraordinary investment: over USD 2 trillion last year alone. While driving jobs and growth the world over.

Friends,

Pointing to progress is not about complacency. It is essential. To combat disinformation and show that this is a fight we can win.

This is the moment to mobilise more. To narrow the gap between pledges and action on the ground.

That will be a central focus of COP31 in Türkiye, and COP32, in Ethiopia next year.

By the second global stocktake in 2028, we must show substantial progress against commitments made in the first. And, from there, identify what’s needed to close the gaps – on both implementation and ambition.

At UN Climate Change, we’re committed to finding ways to help the international process to deliver more. For example, we’re looking at whether countries could designate a representative to coordinate across governments and the private sector – to drive the transition in every industry.

And we are exploring operational opportunities to provide spaces to enhance action. For example, an Action Agenda closing plenary at COPs, alongside the negotiation closing plenaries.

The Action Agenda is a vital part of the work ahead. It's where business, investors, governments, cities and regions, and many more, come together to deliver real economy actions.

In other words, it’s the fast lane to more implementation. Key to helping countries to put their national climate plans into practice.

And there is value in strengthening it within the international process, to complement negotiations, which will remain front and centre.

Getting almost 200 countries to agree on every word is incredibly hard but incredibly important.

No single COP can fix this global crisis, but each takes meaningful steps forward.

COP31 negotiations can support accelerated implementation: enabling stronger institutions and faster technology transfer, improving flow and access to higher-quality finance, and helping countries with their own just transitions.

The Action Agenda can also drive much needed real-world progress.

The Turkish COP31 Presidency – working closely with Australia – has set clear Action Agenda targets, including for electricity to reach 35% of global energy use by 2035.

I urge countries, business leaders, investors and more to respond to the Presidency’s call. And to come to Antalya with solutions that help drive implementation at greater speed and greater scale.

That includes delivering real results to get projects off the ground in developing countries. The UN carbon market is up and running, providing potential new channels for investment.

And our focus this year is meeting existing finance commitments, boosting quality and access. Mobilising every part of the system: from public and private finance, to climate funds, Multilateral Development Banks, and more.

Together, they can get capital flowing, and move the Baku to Belém Roadmap to USD 1.3 trillion closer to reality.

This is no time to backtrack.

This is the time for all shareholders who believe in science, facts, and saving millions of lives to stand firm and step-up on climate.

Friends,

COP31 will be a big tent. Anyone with real solutions is welcome.

The ITA shows that this is what it takes to drive progress.

And your efforts are moving clean industry closer to reality, at scale.

19 commercial-scale projects reached final investment decisions in the first half of this year alone. Together, worth an estimated USD 43 billion.

You are tackling hard problems head on. Which is what this moment demands.

The UNEP Overshoot report is clear.

Bringing global temperature rise back down to 1.5 Celsius will require much greater cuts to planet-heating fossil fuel pollution.

We’ll also need carbon dioxide removals, or CDR – as the IPCC has long assumed – absolutely not as a replacement for transitioning away from all fossil fuels. But in addition to it.

Protecting and enhancing natural carbon sinks will be vital.

Despite some isolated initial efforts, the world is nowhere near ready to deliver, partly due to fears that talk of CDR hands polluters a free pass to continue business as usual.

Many of those fears may well be valid. But simply ignoring CDR is no longer viable.

More policy leaders, investors and innovators need to start tackling this issue – while recognising that transitioning away from fossil fuels can never be circumvented.

Cutting emissions – like building resilience – will always be essential.

Tech titans are increasingly central to that fight.

If AI can solve a 90-year-old math problem in days, it can do more on key climate challenges: building on existing efforts, in areas such as improving early warning systems for climate disasters. And accelerating grid efficiency.

We need every country to benefit from AI today – not vague promises of future solutions.

That means addressing the barriers faced by developing countries. And creating accessible, efficient solutions.

In the world's climate fight, there’s already a worrying two-speed global transition. AI must help bridge, not inflame, this divide.

We also need the industry to respect science and start aligning with global climate efforts – urgently.

Energy guzzling Artificial Intelligence is driving up planet-heating pollution from coal, oil and gas, while ratcheting up energy costs for households and businesses. All while fuelling disinformation, social division, and even larger inequalities of wealth.

AI leaders are now on thin ice when it comes to license to operate, and sinking deep underwater when it comes to public support.

In this country, from the Empire State, to the Lone Star State, datacentres are being put on hold. It’s a similar story in many other parts of the world.

Industry leaders need to step up, including CEOs and boards.

Tech titans need to start showing why the benefits of AI outweigh its skyrocketing costs – for the many, not just the tiny few.

By setting and delivering credible climate targets if they haven’t already.

Investing in efficiency, building on existing gains.

Coming clean about their energy and water use, and powering data-centres with renewable energy – as the UN Secretary-General has said.

Friends,

In almost all places, we're seeing an historic disconnect: between the spiralling scale of the climate crisis impacting billions of daily lives, and the calibre of the response.

This makes no sense, morally, economically or politically.

From the tragedy of the Himalayas. To brutal, economy-slowing heatwaves. And the supercharged impacts of El Niño, set to get worse. The climate crisis is now a national economic and security emergency for all nations.

It should be top of every government's agenda.

Lives and livelihoods are being wrecked. Health impacts and costs are soaring, and health systems are coming under huge strain.

Climate-disasters are hitting crop yields, driving up food prices and wider inflation.

Billions of people around the world are realising that fossil fuel dependence is hitting them hard at the fuel pump each week.

It’s been estimated that since this Middle East conflict began, fossil fuel dependence has heaped over USD 100 billion in extra costs on US consumers alone, just in higher gas and diesel prices.

Any leader serious about combatting inflation, building strong economies, and protecting their citizens, must be serious about cutting the planet-baking fossil fuels driving this climate crisis, and about building resilience.

It's clear now that countries that choose to resist the clean transition aren't protecting old industries – they're sending new innovations, sectors, jobs and pay checks to competitor economies.

Renewables are now cheaper in almost all places. The brute power of market forces is taking hold.

Last year renewables overtook coal as the world's top electricity source.

The shift to clean energy is now irreversible – as all countries at COP30 said in unison.

So friends,

For these reasons and more, we are still absolutely in this fight.

But to win will take far more.

Now's the time to double down on climate multilateralism – the bedrock of the world's progress so far.

At COP30 every nation agreed – the Paris Agreement is working, and we will make it go further and faster.

Let's get to work.

Thank you.
